floors.name: Arrays and the Cost of a Slot

sections.title: One Block, One Multiplication
sections.body:
An array is not a collection of values that happen to be related. It is **one unbroken block of memory** divided into slots of identical width, plus the address where that block begins. Nothing else is stored - there is no table of where each element lives, because there does not need to be one.

That single design decision buys the whole structure: the address of element `i` is $\text{base} + i \times \text{slot}$, one multiplication and one addition regardless of how large `i` is. Reaching element 1,000,000 costs exactly what reaching element 0 costs, which is what **$O(1)$ random access** means.

The price is paid up front and it is real. Every slot must be the same width, so an array of variable-length things stores fixed-width **references** instead of the things themselves. And the block must be unbroken, so the memory has to be found in one piece.

annotations.text: One multiply, one add. There is no loop and no lookup table, and that is the entire reason indexing is O(1).
Index 999999 costs the same arithmetic as index 0. Distance into the array is not work.
JavaScript hides the arithmetic behind a[i], but the engine is doing exactly this for a packed array of numbers.

checkpoint.prompt: A block starts at address 100 and every slot is 4 bytes wide. What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: The base cancels out of any difference of two addresses, so the gap between slot 5 and slot 2 is just 3 slots of 4 bytes. That cancellation is why an array only ever needs to remember one address: everything else is arithmetic on the index.

sections.title: Capacity Is Not Length
sections.body:
A real block of memory has a fixed size, because the bytes on either side of it belong to somebody else. A **dynamic array** is that fixed block wrapped in two numbers: **capacity**, the slots it owns, and **length**, the slots it is using.

`push` is then trivial while `length < capacity`: write into slot `length`, increment `length`. Both are $O(1)$.

When `length === capacity` there is no free slot and the block cannot simply be extended where it sits, so a larger block is allocated, every existing element is copied across, and the old block is released. That push costs $\Theta(n)$ - and it is the only push that does.

annotations.text: The only test that matters. Full means length has caught up with capacity - not that the array is somehow large.
This loop is the expensive push. It touches every element already stored, so it is Theta(length).
The cheap path: one write at slot length, then one increment. Nothing else moves.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete `push`. In order the blanks are: the field `length` is compared against, the factor the capacity is multiplied by, the index the new value is written to, and the operator that advances the count of used slots.
checkpoint.explain: The new value goes at index `length`, not at index `capacity`: `length` is the first unused slot, while `capacity` is one past the last slot the array even owns. Confusing the two writes outside the block, which in a language without bounds checking corrupts whatever lives next door.

sections.title: Amortised $O(1)$, and the $\Theta(n)$ Hiding Inside It
sections.body:
Doubling makes the expensive push rare, and rare in a very specific way. Growing from capacity $c$ copies $c$ elements, and growths happen at capacities $1, 2, 4, \dots$, so the total copying done on the way to $n$ elements is $1 + 2 + 4 + \dots < 2n$. All $n$ pushes together cost $\Theta(n)$, which is $O(1)$ **amortised** - averaged over the sequence, not over any distribution of inputs.

Growing by a constant instead destroys this. Adding one slot at a time copies $1 + 2 + \dots + n = \Theta(n^2)$ elements in total, so each push costs $\Theta(n)$ amortised. **Geometric** growth is the whole trick, and the factor barely matters: 1.5 and 2 are both constants.

Amortised is not a synonym for worst case. One individual push still copies every element, so a system that must answer within a fixed deadline cannot quote the average and call it a bound. The run below shows the two growth rules diverging.

annotations.text: Only the elements already present are copied, so an early growth is cheap and a late one is expensive - but late ones are exponentially rarer.
Change the growth from geometric to additive and every single push reallocates. This one line is the whole difference.
1023 copies against 523776 at n = 1024. Same code otherwise; the growth rule alone decides the asymptotics.

checkpoint.prompt: A dynamic array doubles its capacity whenever it fills. Give the **amortised** cost of a single `push`, and justify it by totalling the copying done across $n$ pushes.
checkpoint.explain: The copying total is a geometric series, 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2, which is under 2n - so n pushes cost Theta(n) altogether and each push costs O(1) on average. The tempting wrong answer is O(n), taken from the worst single push; that push is real, but it can only happen once the array has doubled, so its cost is spread over exponentially many cheap pushes.

sections.title: The Middle Is Expensive, and Two Pointers Are the Answer
sections.body:
The contiguity that makes indexing free is the same contiguity that makes the middle expensive. To insert at index `i` there must be a hole at `i`, so every one of the $n - i$ elements after it moves one slot right; to delete, they all move one slot left. Both are $\Theta(n - i)$, which is $\Theta(n)$ at the front and $\Theta(1)$ at the back.

The direction of the shift is not a matter of taste. Shifting right must run from the last element **downwards**, or each write lands on the element you were about to read and one value smears across the tail.

That cost compounds. Deleting $k$ elements with $k$ separate deletions shifts the tail $k$ times, at $\Theta(nk)$. A **two-pointer** pass does it once: a `read` index sweeps forward while a `write` index trails behind it, and because a slot `read` has already passed is a slot nobody needs again, `write` may overwrite it freely. One pass, $\Theta(n)$ time, no extra memory.

annotations.text: i counts down. Run this loop upwards and arr[i + 1] is overwritten before it is read, smearing one value across the tail.
write only advances on a keeper, so it can never overtake read - which is exactly why overwriting arr[write] is safe.
Shortening by assigning to length is the array equivalent of decrementing a count: the discarded slots simply stop being part of the array.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `isPalindrome(a)` returning `true` when the array reads the same forwards and backwards. Use one index starting at each end and walk them towards each other; do not reverse or copy the array.
checkpoint.explain: Two pointers work here only because indexing is O(1): a[right] is as cheap to read as a[left] no matter how far apart they are. On a linked list the same algorithm would be quadratic. The empty array is true vacuously - the loop never runs - which is the behaviour the `left < right` guard gives you for free.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Writing at index `a.length` is exactly what `push` does: the first unused slot is always at index `length`, and storing there is what makes `length` become 5. The tempting answer for the last line is `4 7`, from assuming the write happened without extending the array - but a dynamic array's length is defined by how many slots are in use, and one more now is.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `addressOf(base, slotSize, index)` returning the memory address of slot `index` in a contiguous block that begins at `base` with slots of `slotSize` bytes. A negative index addresses memory the block does not own, so throw an `Error` whose message contains `index` instead of returning anything.
guided-practice.hint: Slot 0 sits at `base` itself, so the offset is `index * slotSize` and not `(index + 1) * slotSize`.
guided-practice.explain: The whole function is one multiply and one add, and that is the point: no branch depends on how big `index` is, so the work is identical for index 0 and index 1,000,000. The negative case is not pedantry - the arithmetic happily produces an address below the block, and in a language without bounds checking that address is somebody else's data.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete `grow`, which replaces a full block with a larger one. In order the blanks are: the factor the capacity is multiplied by, the field that says how many elements actually need copying, and the field that must be updated to the new size.
guided-practice.explain: The copy loop runs to `length`, not to `capacity`: slots between the two hold nothing worth moving, and copying them would make growth cost the new capacity instead of the old length. Multiplying rather than adding is what turns the total copying into a geometric series instead of a quadratic one.

guided-practice.prompt: A dynamic array is asked to `push` a value at the moment it is completely full. Put the steps in the order they happen.
fragments: Write the new value into slot `length` of the new block
Allocate a new block with twice the capacity
Notice that `length` equals `capacity`, so there is no free slot
Increment `length`
Copy every element already stored into the new block
guided-practice.explain: The copy has to finish before the new value is written, because the new value belongs at index `length`, which only exists inside the new block. A common wrong ordering writes the value first and then reallocates, which would either overflow the old block or copy the new element twice.

guided-practice.prompt: This records the capacity after each of six pushes into an array that starts empty and doubles when full. What does it print?
guided-practice.explain: Capacity changes on pushes 1, 2, 3 and 5 and stays put on 4 and 6, and the gaps between changes double every time. That widening gap is the amortised argument made visible: the expensive pushes thin out exactly as fast as they grow costly.

implementation.prompt: Write `capacityAfter(n)` returning the capacity of a dynamic array after `n` pushes. It starts with capacity 0 and length 0; whenever a push finds `length === capacity` the capacity becomes 1 if it was 0, and otherwise doubles.
implementation.hint: Grow first, then write: the check `length === capacity` happens before the value is stored, so pushing a 9th element into a capacity of 8 doubles it to 16.
implementation.explain: `n = 8` and `n = 9` are the pair that decides whether you understood the rule. Eight pushes exactly fill a capacity of 8 and trigger no growth, because the array only grows when asked for a slot it does not have. Rounding `n` up to the next power of two gives the right answer for every `n` except 0, which is why the zero case is worth a test of its own.

implementation.prompt: Write `totalCopies(n)` returning how many individual element copies a doubling dynamic array performs across `n` pushes, starting empty. Growing copies exactly the elements currently stored - the `length` at that moment, not the capacity.
implementation.hint: The very first growth moves nothing, because the array is empty when it happens. Add `length` before you increment it.
implementation.explain: Look at the answers: 1000 pushes cost 1023 copies and 16 pushes cost 15. The total is always below `2n`, because the copies form the geometric series 1 + 2 + 4 + ... whose sum is under twice its largest term. That bound - not the behaviour of any single push - is what licenses calling push O(1) amortised. The tempting error is `copies += capacity`, which charges for slots holding nothing.

implementation.prompt: Give the **worst-case** cost of a single `push` on a doubling dynamic array holding $n$ elements, and explain why quoting the amortised $O(1)$ would be the wrong answer to this particular question.
implementation.explain: The push that finds the array full allocates a new block and copies all n elements, so its own cost is Theta(n). Amortised O(1) is a statement about a whole sequence of pushes, not a bound on any one of them, and the two answers are each correct to a different question. This matters in practice: a real-time system that must respond within a fixed deadline cannot spend an average, so it pre-sizes the array instead.

implementation.prompt: Write `insertAt(arr, index, value)` returning a **new** array one element longer, with `value` at `index` and everything from `index` onwards moved one slot right. Leave `arr` untouched and do not use `splice`, `slice` or the spread operator - move the elements yourself. An `index` below 0 or above `arr.length` must throw an `Error` whose message contains `range`.
implementation.hint: `index === arr.length` is legal - that is an append, and the tail loop simply runs zero times.
implementation.explain: Inserting at index 0 moves every single element while inserting at the end moves none: the cost is Theta(n - index), which is why an array is a fine queue at the back and a terrible one at the front. Note that `index === arr.length` is valid but `index === arr.length + 1` is not - the legal positions are the gaps between elements, and there are n + 1 of them, not n.

implementation.prompt: Write `removeAll(arr, value)` deleting every occurrence of `value` from `arr` **in place** and returning `arr` itself, using a single forward pass with a read index and a write index. Do not allocate another array, and do not call `splice`, `filter` or `indexOf`. Shorten the array by assigning to `arr.length`.
implementation.hint: `write` only advances when an element survives, so `write <= read` always holds and the slot you write to has already been read.
implementation.explain: Deleting the k matching elements one at a time shifts the tail k times, at Theta(nk); this pass shifts it once, at Theta(n), and uses no extra memory at all. The invariant that makes overwriting safe is `write <= read`: `write` advances only on a survivor, so it can never outrun the read head and never clobbers a slot still waiting to be examined. The `[2,2,2]` case is the one that catches people, because it exercises the final truncation with nothing surviving.

implementation.prompt: This `insertAt` should return a new array with `value` inserted at `index`. `insertAt([1, 2, 4, 5], 2, 3)` should give `[1,2,3,4,5]` but gives `[1,2,3,4,4]`. One line is wrong. Fix it.
implementation.hint: Each iteration writes to a slot the next iteration still needs to read. Run the loop the other way and that stops being true.
implementation.explain: Shifting right must run from the far end downwards. Going upwards, `out[i + 1] = out[i]` destroys `out[i + 1]` before the next iteration reads it, so one value smears across the whole tail. Notice the two append-shaped tests still pass while it is broken: when nothing has to move, direction cannot matter, which is exactly why a single happy-path test would have shipped this bug.

exam.prompt: An array of $n$ numbers is stored as one contiguous block of equal-width slots, with only its base address recorded. Which operation is $O(1)$?
choices: Reading the element at index $n - 1$
Finding the index at which a given value is stored
Inserting a new element at index 0
Deleting the element at index 0
exam.explain: Only the read is arithmetic: base plus index times slot width, done once. Searching must inspect elements until it finds a match, and both edits at index 0 move every remaining element by one slot. The distinction to hold on to is that an array gives you O(1) access **by index** and nothing at all **by value**.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: This push was the cheap kind: there was a spare slot, so it cost one write and one increment. What it also did was leave `length === capacity`, which means the very next push is the expensive one. Capacity does not change when an array fills - only when it is asked to exceed itself.

exam.prompt: Write `reverseInPlace(arr)` reversing `arr` in place and returning `arr` itself, by swapping the outermost pair and walking both indices inward. Do not call `reverse`, and do not build a second array.
exam.hint: `left < right` rather than `left !== right`: on an even length the two indices cross without ever being equal.
exam.explain: Exactly floor(n/2) swaps happen, one per pair, so the pass is Theta(n) with Theta(1) extra space. The guard must be `left < right`: with `left !== right` an even-length array steps straight past equality and the indices run off both ends, and with `left <= right` the middle element of an odd-length array is swapped with itself - harmless here, but the habit is not.

exam.prompt: Give the worst-case running time of inserting one element at index 0 of an array holding $n$ elements, and justify it from what the contiguous layout forces to happen.
exam.explain: Index 0 must be free before the new value can go there, and the only way to free it in a contiguous block is to move all n existing elements one slot right - Theta(n). The tempting answer is O(1), by analogy with reading a[0]; reading needs no slot to be emptied, which is the whole difference. Inserting at the end is the mirror image and costs Theta(1) amortised, because no element has to move at all.

exam.prompt: Explain the mechanism by which storing elements contiguously buys $O(1)$ access by index, and then name two distinct costs the same layout forces on you. Be specific about what the machine actually does.
exam.explain: The mechanism is address arithmetic: base plus index times a fixed slot width, computed once, with no search and no bookkeeping. The costs follow from the same two assumptions. Uniform slot width means anything of variable size must sit behind a reference rather than inline; one unbroken block means the array cannot be extended where it lies, so growing means allocating elsewhere and copying, and inserting or deleting in the middle means shifting the tail. A good answer names the mechanism and at least two of those consequences, not just the phrase O(1).

exam.prompt: Complete the two-pointer reversal. In order the blanks are: the amount subtracted from the length to get the last index, the comparison that stops the walk when the indices meet or cross, and the operator that advances the left index.
exam.explain: `a.length - 1` is the last valid index because slot numbering starts at 0, and `<` is the only safe comparison: on an even length the two indices cross from `left < right` straight to `left > right` without ever being equal, so `!==` would never terminate.

exam.prompt: An empty dynamic array starts with length 0 and capacity 0. Each push writes into slot `length` if one is free, and otherwise first grows the capacity to 1 (if it was 0) or to double its current value. Give `length/capacity` after each push named below, written exactly like `3/4`.
exam.explain: Growth happens on pushes 1, 2, 3, 5 and 9 and nowhere else, and those are exactly the pushes numbered one more than a power of two. Notice that pushes 4 and 8 both fill the block completely without growing it: an array grows when it is asked for a slot it does not own, not when it runs out of spare ones.

exam.prompt: A dynamic array grows by exactly **one** slot each time it fills, copying every stored element into the new block. What is the amortised cost of a single `push`?
choices: $\Theta(1)$
$\Theta(\log n)$
$\Theta(n)$
$\Theta(n \log n)$
exam.explain: Every push reallocates, copying 0, then 1, then 2, ... elements, so n pushes cost 1 + 2 + ... + (n-1) = Theta(n^2) in total and Theta(n) each on average. The tempting answer is Theta(1), carried over from the doubling case - but doubling earns that bound precisely because the growths become exponentially rarer, and additive growth makes them universal instead.

exam.prompt: Write `moveZeroesToEnd(arr)` moving every `0` to the back of `arr` **in place**, returning `arr` itself, with the non-zero elements keeping their original relative order. Use one read index and one write index; do not allocate another array and do not use `filter`, `sort` or `splice`.
exam.hint: After the compacting pass, `write` is the count of non-zeroes - which is also the first index that still needs a zero written into it.
exam.explain: This is the compaction pass from `removeAll` with a second loop that refills the tail instead of truncating it, and the same `write <= read` invariant is what makes overwriting safe. Order preservation is not a bonus: it comes from `read` sweeping strictly forward, so survivors are written in the order they were met. Swapping each zero with the last element would also move every zero to the back, in the same Theta(n), but would scramble the rest - a reminder that the same big-O can hide entirely different behaviour.

exam.prompt: An array of `length` elements is asked to delete the element at index `i` and hand it back. Put the steps in the order they happen.
fragments: Decrement `length`, so the last slot is no longer part of the array
Copy `a[j]` into `a[j - 1]` for every `j` from `i + 1` up to `length - 1`
Check that `i` is a valid index, and stop if it is not
Read the value stored at index `i` so it can be returned
exam.explain: The value has to be read before the shift, because the shift is what overwrites slot `i` - reading afterwards returns its replacement. Decrementing `length` must come last, since the loop's upper bound is expressed in terms of the old length. Note that nothing is erased: the duplicate left in the final slot simply stops being addressable, which is why deleting from an array frees no memory at all.

sections.title: A Node, a Head, and the Null at the End
sections.body:
An array is one contiguous block of memory, so element $i$ is found by arithmetic: base address plus $i$ times the element size. A **linked list** gives that up. It stores each value in its own separately allocated **node**, and each node holds a `next` reference to the following node, so the elements can sit anywhere in memory at all.

That buys one thing and costs another. You no longer need a single block big enough for everything, and you can splice a node in without shifting anything - but the only way to reach the $i$th element is to start at the **head**, the reference to the first node, and follow `next` $i$ times.

The chain has to end somewhere, and the marker is `null`: the last node's `next` is `null`, and an empty list is a head that is `null`. Every traversal you will ever write is the same three lines - start at the head, do something, step to `next` - and it stops precisely when it meets that `null`.

annotations.text: The chain is built back to front, because b cannot point at c until c exists. c.next is null: this is the last node.
The loop condition IS the null terminator. Nothing else tells you where the list stops - there is no length to compare against.
The only move available is forward, one link at a time. There is no node.prev here and no node[i] anywhere.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `listLength(head)` returning how many nodes the list contains. `head` is a node `{ value, next }` or `null` for an empty list.
checkpoint.explain: Counting is $O(n)$ here, not $O(1)$ - unless the list separately caches a length, the only way to know how long it is, is to walk it. An array knows its own length because it was allocated as one block; a chain of nodes knows nothing but its own first link.

sections.title: Free at the Head, Dear at the Tail
sections.body:
Inserting at the head is the operation linked lists exist for. Make a node, point its `next` at the current head, and call the new node the head: three assignments, no walking, no shifting, $O(1)$ regardless of how long the list already is.

Inserting at the **tail** is the opposite. With only a head reference you cannot get to the last node without walking every link to find it, so a single append is $\Theta(n)$ and building an $n$-element list by repeated appending costs $0 + 1 + \dots + (n-1) = \Theta(n^2)$.

The fix is to keep a second reference, a **tail** pointer, alongside the head. Then appending is $O(1)$ too, at the price of one more variable to keep correct on every single insert and delete - and a stale tail pointer is a far nastier bug than a slow append.

Notice in the run below that pushing $1..5$ onto the head produces the list in reverse. Head insertion is not just cheap, it is order-reversing, which is exactly why it is the natural way to build a stack.

annotations.text: The whole of head insertion. The old head is not modified at all - it simply becomes the second node.
This walk is the entire cost of appending. It touches every existing node just to find the one whose next is null.
Six walk steps to append five values, and the count grows quadratically. A tail pointer would make it zero.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `push(head, value)` returning the head of a list with a new node holding `value` in front of the existing list. Do not modify any existing node.
checkpoint.explain: The `null` case needs no special handling, and that is the point: an empty list is just a head of `null`, so `{ value: 1, next: null }` falls out of the same expression that handles a list of a million nodes. Code that tests `if (head === null)` here is doing work the representation already did.

sections.title: To Delete a Node You Need the One Before It
sections.body:
Deleting node $x$ means making the node **before** $x$ point past it - `prev.next = x.next`. Nothing frees $x$ explicitly; once no `next` refers to it, it is unreachable and the garbage collector takes it.

In a singly linked list that predecessor is not obtainable from $x$ itself. Even if somebody hands you a direct reference to the node you want gone, you must start at the head and walk until you find the node whose `next` is $x$ - so deletion costs $\Theta(n)$ even when you already know exactly what to remove.

The head is the exception and the classic bug: it has no predecessor, so removing it means returning `head.next` as the new head rather than re-pointing anything. Forget that case and your function silently refuses to delete the first element.

A **doubly linked** list gives every node a `prev` as well as a `next`. Now the predecessor is one dereference away and unlinking a known node is $O(1)$ - paid for with an extra reference per node and two pointers to fix, in both directions, on every insert and delete.

annotations.text: The head case. It cannot be handled by the loop below, because there is no node whose next points at the head.
The search for the predecessor. This walk, not the unlinking, is what makes singly linked deletion linear.
With a prev reference the predecessor is simply b.prev - no search at all. That is the whole of what doubly linked buys.

checkpoint.prompt: Three nodes are chained `1 -> 2 -> 3`, then one line changes a link. What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: Node `b` is untouched - it still holds 2 and still points at `c`. Deletion in a linked list never edits the deleted node; it edits the node in front of it, and `b` disappears only because nothing reachable refers to it any more.

sections.title: Reversing in Place, and What a Chain Is Actually Good At
sections.body:
Reversal is the exercise that proves you understand links. Walk the list once carrying two references, `prev` and `cur`, and flip each `cur.next` to point backwards at `prev`. The one line everybody forgets is saving `cur.next` into a temporary **before** overwriting it - overwrite first and you have just destroyed the only route to the rest of the list.

It is $\Theta(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space: no new nodes, no copying, just $n$ pointer flips. When the loop ends `cur` is `null` and `prev` is sitting on the old last node, which is the new head - so you return `prev`, not `cur` and not `head`.

So when is a chain actually better than a block? When you insert and delete at known positions in a long sequence and rarely index into it - a queue, a stack, an LRU eviction list, the free list in an allocator. Splicing costs $O(1)$ once you hold the right node, while an array insert shifts everything after it.

And when is it worse? Almost everywhere else. There is no random access, so `list[i]` becomes an $O(i)$ walk. Every node is a separate allocation, so the elements are scattered and each hop is a potential cache miss, whereas an array walk pulls in whole cache lines of useful data at once. In practice an array often wins even at the theoretical tasks, because a constant factor of ten or more from **cache locality** beats a better exponent at any size you are likely to have.

annotations.text: Save the forward link before you destroy it. Without this line the next iteration has nowhere to go.
The flip itself. Every other line exists only to keep this one from stranding the rest of the list.
Two hops to reach index 2, and it would be a million hops for index 1000000. No arithmetic can shortcut a chain.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the in-place reversal. In order the blanks are: what `prev` starts as, the field saved into `next` before it is overwritten, what `cur.next` is flipped to point at, and the reference returned as the new head.
checkpoint.explain: `prev` starts at `null` because the old head becomes the new tail, and a tail's `next` must be `null` - the terminator is created by that initial value, not by a special case at the end. Returning `head` instead of `prev` is the other stock mistake: `head` is by then the last node, so you get a one-element list.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: The `for` loop is an ordinary traversal in disguise: the initialiser is the head, the test is the null terminator, and the update step is the link. It visits every node exactly once and stops the instant `n` becomes `null`, which is why 4 + 8 + 15 = 27 and not an infinite loop.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the traversal that collects every value into an array. In order the blanks are: where the walk starts, the value the walk stops at, and the field holding the payload.
guided-practice.explain: Walking with a separate `node` variable rather than reassigning `head` matters: reassigning the parameter loses the caller's grip on the front of the list, and in a longer function you then have no way back to the start. The `null` test is the only stopping condition available, because nothing in the list records its own length.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `toArray(head)` returning a plain array of every value in the list, front to back. `head` is a node `{ value, next }` or `null`.

tests.input: { value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }

guided-practice.hint: One loop variable, starting at `head`, advancing with `n = n.next`, stopping at `null`.
guided-practice.explain: The empty case is the one to get right, and it needs no branch: a head of `null` fails the loop test immediately and the empty `out` is returned. Any solution that reads `head.value` before testing for `null` throws on exactly that input.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `pushAll(values)` that starts from an empty list and pushes each element of the array `values` onto the **head** in turn, returning the resulting head. `pushAll([1, 2, 3])` therefore returns the list `3 -> 2 -> 1`. Return `null` for an empty array.
guided-practice.hint: `head = { value: v, next: head };` - the old head becomes the second node, and the variable is rebound to the new one.
guided-practice.explain: The output comes out reversed, and that is not a bug to fix but the defining behaviour of head insertion: each new node is placed in front of everything already there. It is also why the head must be a variable you rebind - the head of a linked list is not a fixed node, it is whichever node currently happens to be first.

guided-practice.prompt: Put the steps of appending a value to the **tail** of a singly linked list, given only a head reference, into the order they execute.
fragments: Walk `cur` forward while `cur.next` is not null
Return the original head, which still points at the same first node
Build a new node holding the value, with `next` set to null
If the head is null, return the new node as the whole list
Point `cur.next` at the new node
guided-practice.explain: The empty-list test has to come before the walk, because there is no `cur` to start walking from - that check is what stops a null dereference rather than being defensive decoration. The head is returned unchanged because appending never touches the front of the list, which is the asymmetry that makes tail insertion the expensive end.

guided-practice.prompt: This builds a six-element list by appending one value at a time, counting every link it has to follow. What does it print?
guided-practice.explain: The appends walk 0, 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 links, summing to 10 - the arithmetic series $0 + 1 + \dots + (n-2)$, which is $\Theta(n^2)$ for $n$ appends. The tempting answer 6 comes from counting appends instead of links; the whole point is that the cost of one append depends on how much list is already there.

implementation.prompt: Write `append(head, value)` adding a new node holding `value` at the **end** of the list and returning the head of the resulting list. Appending to an empty list (`null`) returns the new node.

tests.input: { value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 4

implementation.hint: Stop the walk at the node whose `next` is null - that is the last node. Stopping when `cur` itself is null overshoots and leaves you nothing to attach to.
implementation.explain: The loop condition must be `cur.next !== null`, not `cur !== null`: you need to stop **on** the last node, not one past it, because a null `cur` has no `next` to assign to. That off-by-one is the append bug, and the empty-list branch exists because there is no last node to stop on at all.

implementation.prompt: Write `removeAt(head, index)` removing the node at the zero-based `index` and returning the head of the resulting list. If `index` is negative or past the end, return the list unchanged. Removing index 0 returns the second node as the new head.

tests.input: { value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 0
{ value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 1
{ value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 2
{ value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 5
{ value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, -1

implementation.hint: Walk `prev` forward `index - 1` times so it lands on the node **before** the target, then splice with `prev.next = prev.next.next`.
implementation.explain: Index 0 cannot go through the splice at all, because the head has no predecessor to re-point - it is removed by returning a different head. The out-of-range tests matter for the same reason the walk needs a guard: run off the end and `prev` becomes `null`, and `prev.next` then throws rather than quietly doing nothing.

implementation.prompt: `removeValue(head, value)` should remove the first node holding `value` and return the head of the resulting list. It works for values in the middle, but `removeValue({ value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: null } }, 1)` returns the list still containing 1, and calling it on an empty list throws. Fix it.

tests.input: { value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 2
{ value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 1
{ value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 3
{ value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 9

implementation.hint: The loop can only ever look at `prev.next`, so the head is the one node it can never inspect. Two guards before the loop fix both symptoms.
implementation.explain: The loop starts at the head and only ever examines `prev.next`, so the head itself is never a candidate for removal - the function is structurally blind to the first element. The null case throws for the same underlying reason: the code assumes a predecessor exists before it has checked that any node exists at all.

implementation.prompt: Write `reverse(head)` reversing the list **in place** - reusing the existing nodes, allocating no new ones - and returning the head of the reversed list. `reverse(null)` returns `null`.

tests.input: { value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }

implementation.hint: Four lines inside the loop, and the first must save `cur.next` before the second overwrites it.
implementation.explain: Starting `prev` at `null` is what gives the old head its new terminator, and returning `prev` rather than `cur` is what gives you the old tail - when the loop exits `cur` is always `null`, so returning it always yields an empty list. The single-node case is the cheap check that your loop does not depend on there being a second node.

implementation.prompt: Build a **doubly linked** list from the array `values`, where every node is `{ value, prev, next }`, then read it back twice: forwards from the head and backwards from the tail. Write `doublyBothWays(values)` returning `{ forwards, backwards }`, two plain arrays. For `[1, 2, 3]` that is `{ forwards: [1, 2, 3], backwards: [3, 2, 1] }`. An empty array gives two empty arrays.
implementation.hint: Keeping `tail` as you build is what makes each append $O(1)$; the new node's `prev` is the old tail, and the old tail's `next` is the new node.
implementation.explain: Every insert now maintains two links instead of one, and both must be set or the backwards walk quietly returns a shorter list than the forwards one - a doubly linked list that disagrees with itself is the characteristic failure here. Note that the backwards read is only possible because a tail reference was kept: `prev` links alone are useless if you cannot reach the last node.

implementation.prompt: You build an $n$-element list by calling `append` once per value on a singly linked list that keeps only a head reference. Give the total running time of all $n$ appends, justify it from the cost of a single append, and say what keeping a tail reference changes.
implementation.explain: One append must walk from the head to the last node, so the $k$th append costs $\Theta(k)$, and summing $0 + 1 + \dots + (n-1)$ gives $\Theta(n^2)$. A tail pointer removes the walk entirely and each append becomes $O(1)$, giving $\Theta(n)$ overall - the same asymptotic total as pushing at the head, which is the honest comparison. The tempting answer is $O(n)$, from reading 'append is one operation' rather than pricing the search it hides.

exam.prompt: What does this print? Both lines of output, in order.
exam.explain: Moving a head variable moves only that variable - no node was modified, so `list` still reaches all three values. This is why deletion has to re-point the predecessor's `next` and not merely advance some local reference: a reference is a way in, not the list itself.

exam.prompt: In a singly linked list, what marks the end of the chain?
choices: A node whose `value` is null
A node whose `next` is null
A length field stored on the head node
A node whose `next` points back at the head
exam.explain: The terminator is a property of the link, not of the payload: `next === null` says there is nothing after this node, while a null `value` is a perfectly legal element in the middle of a list. The last option describes a circular list, where a traversal that tests for `null` never terminates at all.

exam.prompt: Write `nodeAt(head, index)` returning the **value** stored at the zero-based `index`, or `null` if the index is negative or beyond the end of the list.

tests.input: { value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 0
{ value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 2
{ value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, 3
{ value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }, -1

exam.hint: Check for `null` inside the hop loop as well as after it, or an index one past the end throws instead of returning null.
exam.explain: This function is $\Theta(index)$ where the array equivalent `arr[i]` is $O(1)$, and no cleverness removes the gap: an array computes an address, a list must follow links it cannot predict. That difference is what makes an innocent-looking `for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) nodeAt(head, i)` a quadratic loop over a structure a single traversal would cover in linear time.

exam.prompt: Complete the removal of the first node holding `value`. In order the blanks are: what is returned for an empty list, what is returned when the head itself matches, the field compared against `value` during the search, and the link `prev.next` is re-pointed at.
exam.explain: The search inspects `prev.next.value` rather than `prev.value` because you must stop on the node **before** the match - stopping on the match itself leaves you holding a node you cannot unlink. `prev.next = prev.next.next` is the splice, and it is the only line that actually deletes anything.

exam.prompt: Trace the in-place reversal of `1 -> 2 -> 3`. `prev` starts as `null` and `cur` at the head; each iteration saves `cur.next`, sets `cur.next = prev`, then moves `prev` to `cur` and `cur` to the saved node. After each iteration give the list you get by following `next` from `prev` (written as `[3,2,1]`), and the value at `cur` (write `null` if `cur` is null).
exam.explain: `prev` grows into the finished reversed list one node per iteration while `cur` marches down what is left of the original, so at every moment the list is split into a reversed prefix and an untouched suffix. That invariant is why the loop is correct, and why `cur` reaching `null` - not `prev` - is the stopping condition.

exam.prompt: Inserting at the front of an array is $\Theta(n)$ because every later element shifts, while inserting at the front of a linked list is $O(1)$. Explain why, despite this, iterating over a large linked list is routinely slower in practice than iterating over an array of the same values.
exam.explain: Asymptotics count operations and assume each costs the same, and that assumption is wrong on real hardware. An array is contiguous, so one cache line fetch delivers several elements and the prefetcher can predict the next one; a linked list's nodes are separate allocations scattered across memory, and each hop must load the pointer before it knows which address to fetch next - a dependency chain of potential cache misses. The lesson is not that big-O lies, but that it prices operations, not memory traffic.

exam.prompt: Which job does a singly linked list genuinely do better than a JavaScript array?
choices: Reading the 500000th element
Repeatedly adding and removing at the front of a long sequence
Summing every element as quickly as possible
Sorting the elements without allocating extra memory
exam.explain: Front insertion and removal are $O(1)$ on a list and $\Theta(n)$ on an array, because an array must shift every remaining element. The other three all favour the array: indexing is $O(1)$ against $\Theta(i)$, and summing or sorting both walk memory, where contiguity and cache locality win even though the operation counts match.

exam.prompt: Put the steps of removing the first node holding a given value from a singly linked list into the order they execute.
fragments: Set `prev.next` to `prev.next.next`, unlinking the matched node
If the head itself holds the value, return `head.next` as the new head
Return the head, unchanged unless it was the node removed
Walk `prev` forward while `prev.next` exists and does not hold the value
Return null immediately if the list is empty
exam.explain: Both guards must precede the walk: the empty test because there is no node to start from, and the head test because the walk can only ever inspect `prev.next` and so can never see the first node. Leave either out and you get the two classic deletion bugs - a crash on the empty list, and a first element that refuses to be removed.

sections.title: The stack: one end, three operations
sections.body:
A **stack** is a list you are only allowed to touch at one end. Three operations, and no others: `push` puts a value on the top, `pop` takes the top value off and returns it, and `peek` looks at the top without removing it. Nothing reaches into the middle. That restriction is not a limitation the designer failed to remove - it is the entire point, because it is what makes every operation O(1).

The discipline this enforces is **LIFO**: last in, first out. The most recently pushed value is the first one you get back. If you push `1`, `2`, `3` and then pop three times, you get `3`, `2`, `1` - the reverse of the order you put them in. A stack is therefore a reversing machine, which is why so many uses of it are really "undo the most recent thing first".

In JavaScript an array is already a perfectly good stack, because `push` and `pop` both operate on the **end** of the array. That matters: the end is the cheap end. Adding or removing at the end shifts nothing, so it is O(1). Adding or removing at the front with `unshift` or `shift` has to move every other element along by one, so it is O(n). A stack is fast precisely because it never asks for the expensive end.

annotations.text: Peek is just an index read. There is no built-in `peek`, so you index the last slot - and you must guard the empty case, because `stack[-1]` is `undefined`, not an error.
`pop` returns the value it removed. Popping an empty array also returns `undefined` rather than throwing, which is a common source of silent bugs.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete `peek`, which returns the top of the stack without removing it, and `null` if the stack is empty.
checkpoint.explain: The top of a stack backed by an array is the LAST slot, and the last index is `length - 1`, not `length` - indexing at `length` is one past the end and yields `undefined`. The empty guard matters because `stack[-1]` is also `undefined`, so without it a caller cannot tell an empty stack from a stack whose top really is `undefined`.

sections.title: What a stack is actually for
sections.body:
The reversing behaviour is useful, but the deeper use is **matching**: whenever something opens and must later close in the opposite order, a stack is the structure that remembers what is still open.

Bracket matching is the clearest case. Read left to right; every opening bracket gets pushed, and every closing bracket must match whatever is on top. If it does not match, or the stack is empty when a closer arrives, the string is unbalanced. If anything is left on the stack at the end, something was opened and never closed. Note what this catches that mere counting does not: `([)]` has exactly one of each bracket, so any count-based check passes it, but it is plainly wrong. Order is the thing being checked, and a stack is what holds order.

The same shape is everywhere once you see it. Your language's **call stack** pushes a frame per call and pops it on return, which is why the most recent call is the one that returns first. Undo history pops the most recent edit. Depth-first search pushes the frontier and pops the deepest node. Expression evaluation in reverse Polish notation pushes operands and pops them in pairs as operators arrive.

annotations.text: One line does two jobs: it rejects a mismatched closer, AND it rejects a closer arriving at an empty stack, because `pop()` on an empty array returns `undefined`, which never equals a bracket character.
The final check is what catches `'((('`. Every character was legal on its own; the string is still unbalanced because something was opened and never closed.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: Only `(` is ever pushed, and the string contains one, so the stack ends with a single item and `length === 0` is `false`. This is the leftover-opener case: nothing in the string was illegal as it was read, yet the string is unbalanced, which is exactly why the final emptiness check cannot be dropped.

sections.title: The queue: two ends, and one of them is expensive
sections.body:
A **queue** is the other restriction: you add at one end and remove from the other. `enqueue` puts a value at the back, `dequeue` takes one from the front. That gives **FIFO** - first in, first out, the discipline of an actual queue of people. Where a stack reverses, a queue preserves order.

The obvious JavaScript implementation is an array with `push` to enqueue and `shift` to dequeue, and it is a trap. `push` is O(1), but `shift` removes the element at index 0 and then moves every remaining element down one slot to close the gap - that is O(n). Draining a queue of n items that way costs O(n²) overall. It is fine for ten items and quietly ruinous for a hundred thousand.

The fix is a **circular buffer**: a fixed array plus two indices, `head` and `tail`, that chase each other around it. Dequeuing does not move any data; it just advances `head`, wrapping to 0 when it runs off the end via `(head + 1) % capacity`. Nothing is shifted, so both ends are O(1). The cost is that you must track how many items are live, because `head === tail` is ambiguous on its own - it means both empty and completely full.

annotations.text: The modulo IS the circle. When `tail` reaches `capacity` it wraps to 0 and reuses slots that have already been dequeued, which is what stops the buffer walking off the end of the array.
Dequeue moves an index, not data. This single line is the whole reason a circular buffer is O(1) where `Array.shift` is O(n).

checkpoint.prompt: Write `drainQueue(items)` which enqueues every value in the array `items` and then dequeues them all, returning an array of the values in the order they came out. Use FIFO order. An empty input returns an empty array.
checkpoint.explain: A queue preserves order, so what comes out is exactly what went in - which is why this looks like it does nothing. That is the point: the test that distinguishes a queue from a stack is precisely whether the output is the input or its reverse. Had you used `pop` instead of `shift`, `[1, 2, 3]` would have come back as `[3, 2, 1]`.
checkpoint.hint: Enqueue with `push` at the back; dequeue with `shift` from the front. If you reach for `pop` you have built a stack.

sections.title: Deques, and a queue built from two stacks
sections.body:
A **deque** - double-ended queue - drops the restriction entirely and allows push and pop at both ends. It subsumes both structures: use one end and it is a stack, use both and it is a queue. Implemented over a circular buffer, all four operations are O(1). The trade is that the restriction was doing useful work: a stack's API makes it impossible to write the bug where you accidentally read from the wrong end.

There is one more construction worth knowing, because of what it teaches about cost. You can build a FIFO queue out of two LIFO stacks. Everything enqueued is pushed onto an `inbox` stack. To dequeue, if the `outbox` stack is empty, pour the entire inbox into it - popping each item and pushing it - which reverses the order, so the oldest item ends up on top of the outbox. Then pop the outbox.

That pour is O(n), so a single dequeue can be expensive. But each element is moved from inbox to outbox **exactly once** in its whole lifetime, and is then popped once. Over any sequence of operations the total work is proportional to the number of elements, so the cost per operation **averaged over the sequence** is O(1). This is **amortised** analysis, and it is a different claim from "every operation is fast". It says the expensive steps are rare enough that they are paid for by the cheap ones - the same argument that justifies a dynamic array's doubling.

annotations.text: Popping from one stack while pushing to another reverses the order. Two reversals - once in, once out - restore the original order, which is how two LIFO structures compose into a FIFO one.

The guard is what makes the amortised argument work. Pouring only when the outbox is EMPTY guarantees each element is moved at most once; pouring every time would move elements repeatedly and the bound would collapse.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `dequeAlternate(items)`. Push every value of `items` onto the **back** of a deque, then repeatedly remove from the front and the back alternately - front first - collecting the removed values into an array. For `[1, 2, 3, 4]` that yields `[1, 4, 2, 3]`. An empty input returns an empty array.
checkpoint.explain: The odd-length case is the one that catches people: with `[1, 2, 3]` the front takes 1, the back takes 3, and then a single element remains, which the front takes. If you do not re-check emptiness between the two removals in a single pass, that last element gets taken twice or the loop runs off the end.
checkpoint.hint: Re-check that the deque is non-empty between the front removal and the back removal, or an odd-length input takes its last element twice.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Track the top, not the whole history. After push 1, 2 the stack is `[1,2]`; the pop removes 2 leaving `[1]`; push 3, 4 gives `[1,3,4]`; the final pop removes 4, the most recent, leaving `[1,3]`. The tempting wrong answer is `1,4` - it comes from imagining that a pop removes the OLDEST item, which is what a queue would do.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: `push` adds at the back and `shift` removes from the front, so this is a queue. The first `shift` removes 'a'; 'c' joins the back behind 'b'; the second `shift` therefore returns 'b'. Answering 'c' means reading `shift` as `pop` - the exact confusion the two structures exist to keep apart.

guided-practice.prompt: Trace `isBalanced('([{}])')` from the lesson. After each character is read, what does the stack contain, written top-last (so `([` means `(` at the bottom and `[` on top)? Give the empty stack as an empty string.
guided-practice.explain: The stack grows to its full depth at the innermost point and then unwinds symmetrically. That symmetry is the visible shape of nesting: the stack height at any moment is exactly the current nesting depth, and a balanced string is one whose height returns to zero having never gone below it.

guided-practice.prompt: Put the steps of a circular-buffer `dequeue` into the order they must happen.
fragments: if the buffer is empty, return null
read the value at index `head`
advance `head` to `(head + 1) % capacity`
decrement `size`
return the value that was read
guided-practice.explain: The value must be read BEFORE `head` moves, because once `head` has advanced it points at the next item and the one you wanted is no longer addressable. Advancing first and reading after is the single most common way to write this wrong, and it fails silently by returning the wrong element rather than crashing.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the wrap-around arithmetic for a circular buffer's `enqueue`.
guided-practice.explain: The modulus is the buffer's fixed `capacity`, never its current `size` - taking the modulus by `size` would make the wrap point move as the queue filled and drained, and slots would be overwritten while still holding live data. `size` is tracked separately precisely because `head === tail` cannot by itself distinguish an empty buffer from a full one.

guided-practice.prompt: A colleague implements a queue as a JavaScript array using `push` to enqueue and `shift` to dequeue. It passes every test. Explain what is wrong with it, what the cost is, and what you would change.
guided-practice.explain: It is correct but not fast. `Array.shift` removes the element at index 0 and then relocates every remaining element down one slot, so it is O(n) rather than O(1), and draining n items costs O(n²). Tests do not catch it because the behaviour is right - only the cost is wrong, and cost is invisible until the input grows. The fix is to stop moving data: a circular buffer with `head` and `tail` indices, or a linked list with a tail pointer, makes both ends O(1).

implementation.prompt: Write `isBalanced(s)` returning `true` if every bracket in the string `s` is closed by the matching kind in the correct order. Handle `()`, `[]` and `{}`. Non-bracket characters are ignored. The empty string is balanced.
implementation.explain: Three distinct failures have to be caught and they are easy to conflate: a wrong-kind closer (`([)]`), a leftover opener (`(((`), and a closer with nothing open (`)(`). The last is the one people miss, because `[].pop()` returns `undefined` rather than throwing - so comparing the popped value against the expected opener handles it for free, whereas checking `stack.length` first and popping after does not.
implementation.hint: Comparing `stack.pop()` against the expected opener handles the empty-stack case for free, because popping an empty array gives `undefined`.

implementation.prompt: Write `evalRPN(tokens)` evaluating an array of reverse-Polish tokens. Each token is either an integer as a string or one of `'+'`, `'-'`, `'*'`, `'/'`. Push operands; on an operator, pop two and push the result. Division truncates towards zero. Return the final value.
implementation.explain: The order of the two pops is the whole exercise. The FIRST value popped is the RIGHT-hand operand, because it was pushed most recently - so subtraction must be `a - b` where `b` came off first. Getting it backwards still passes `['2','3','+']`, since addition commutes, and fails only on `-` and `/`; that is why the test set includes both.
implementation.hint: The first value you pop is the right-hand operand. Name the two pops `b` then `a` and the subtraction writes itself.

implementation.prompt: Write `firstUnique(s)` returning the first character of the string `s` that appears exactly once, or `null` if there is no such character. Use a queue of candidates: discard from the front while the front is known to be repeated.
implementation.explain: A queue is the right structure because the answer must be the EARLIEST such character, and a queue is the structure that preserves arrival order. The two edge cases pull in opposite directions: `'aabb'` drains the queue completely and must yield `null`, while `'z'` must not be discarded despite never being compared against anything else.
implementation.hint: Count every character before you queue anything - you cannot know whether the first character is unique until you have seen the last.

implementation.prompt: Write `twoStackQueue(ops)` implementing a FIFO queue using only two arrays as stacks - `push` and `pop` only, never `shift` or `unshift`. `ops` is an array of strings: `'push N'` enqueues the integer N, and `'pop'` dequeues. Return an array of the values produced by the `'pop'` operations, using `null` when the queue is empty.
implementation.explain: The condition on the pour is what makes this correct AND fast. Pouring only when the outbox is empty keeps the interleaved case right - in test 3, item 1 is dequeued before 2 and 3 are ever enqueued, and they must still come out in order - and it guarantees each element moves between stacks exactly once, which is the amortised O(1) argument. Pouring unconditionally on every dequeue would reverse a partially-drained outbox and produce LIFO output.
implementation.hint: Pour only when the outbox is empty. Pouring on every dequeue buries older items under newer ones and breaks FIFO order.

implementation.prompt: Write `minStack(ops)` supporting `'push N'`, `'pop'` and `'min'`, where `'min'` reports the smallest value currently on the stack in O(1) - without scanning. Return an array of the values reported by the `'min'` operations, using `null` if the stack is empty.
implementation.explain: The trick is a second stack pushed in lockstep, each entry holding the minimum of everything at or below it - so popping the value stack and the minimum stack together restores the previous minimum for free. The duplicate case `['push 2','push 2', ...]` is why you push the minimum on EVERY push rather than only when a new record is set: with only-on-record, popping one of the two 2s would wrongly discard the minimum still in force.
implementation.hint: Push onto the minimum stack on every push, even when the value is not a new minimum - otherwise popping a duplicate discards a minimum that is still in force.

implementation.prompt: This checker counts brackets instead of stacking them, so it accepts strings it should reject. Fix it so it checks order as well as count, keeping the name `isBalancedCount`.
implementation.explain: Counters record how many are open but not which is innermost, and nesting is a question about order. `([)]` has one of each bracket so both counters return to zero; `)(` does too, which is why a counter-based check also accepts a string that closes before it opens. Only a stack retains the sequence, and replacing the two counters with one stack fixes both failures at once.
implementation.hint: The two counters cannot be repaired - they record how many are open, never which is innermost. Replace them with one stack.

exam.prompt: Which discipline does a stack enforce?
choices: LIFO - the most recently added item is removed first
FIFO - the earliest added item is removed first
Sorted order - the smallest item is removed first
Random access - any item may be removed by index
exam.explain: LIFO is the defining property. FIFO describes a queue, smallest-first describes a priority queue or heap, and indexed access describes an array - each is a different contract, and the whole value of naming the structure is that the name tells a reader which one holds.

exam.prompt: What is the time complexity of `Array.prototype.shift` on an array of n elements?
choices: O(n), because every remaining element moves down one slot
O(1), because it only changes the length
O(log n), because the array is indexed
O(n log n), because the array is re-sorted
exam.explain: Removing the element at index 0 leaves a hole that has to be closed, so every later element is relocated - linear work. This is the trap in the naive array queue: `push` really is O(1), so the structure looks cheap until you notice that only one of its two operations is.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: Pushing then popping everything reverses the sequence, because the last thing in is the first thing out. This is the shortest demonstration that a stack is a reversing machine - and it is why two stacks in series, each reversing once, compose into a FIFO queue.

exam.prompt: Complete the pour step of a queue built from two stacks.
exam.explain: The guard must be emptiness, not a count or a flag: pouring into a non-empty outbox would bury older items beneath newer ones and break FIFO order. Popping the inbox while pushing the outbox is what performs the reversal that turns two LIFO stacks into one FIFO queue.

exam.prompt: Order these operations so that the final value returned is `1`, starting from an empty stack-based structure that reverses its input twice.
fragments: enqueue 1
enqueue 2
pour the inbox into the empty outbox, reversing it
pop the outbox
exam.explain: Both values must be enqueued before the pour, because the pour reverses whatever the inbox holds at that moment. With 1 and 2 in the inbox as `[1,2]`, pouring produces an outbox of `[2,1]` whose top is 1 - the oldest item, exactly as FIFO requires.

exam.prompt: A circular buffer has `capacity` 3, and starts with `head` 0, `tail` 0, `size` 0. Give `head`, `tail` and `size` as three comma-separated numbers after each operation.
exam.explain: The fourth step is the one that shows the structure working: `tail` reaches 3, wraps to 0 via the modulus, and reuses the slot that the dequeue freed. Note that after the last step `head` and `tail` are both 1 while `size` is 3 - the buffer is full, and `head === tail` here means full rather than empty, which is exactly why `size` must be tracked separately.

exam.prompt: A queue is built from two stacks, as in the lesson. Over a sequence of n enqueues followed by n dequeues, what is the amortised cost per operation? Give the complexity, then justify it.
exam.explain: A single dequeue can cost O(n) when it triggers the pour, so the worst-case-per-operation answer is O(n) - but that is not what was asked. Each element is pushed to the inbox once, moved to the outbox once, and popped once: three constant-time steps per element, so 2n operations do O(n) total work and the amortised cost is O(1). The distinction matters in practice: this is fine for throughput and unacceptable for a hard real-time deadline, where one unlucky dequeue blows the budget.

exam.prompt: Write `decodeUndo(ops)` where `ops` is an array of strings: `'type X'` appends the character X to a document, and `'undo'` removes the most recent still-standing `type`. Return the final document as a string. An `'undo'` on an empty document does nothing.
exam.explain: Undo is the canonical stack application because 'most recent' and 'top of stack' are the same idea. The edge case that matters is undoing past the beginning - `['type a','undo','undo']` - where popping an already-empty array returns `undefined` rather than throwing, so a careless implementation appends the string 'undefined' to the document instead of doing nothing.
exam.hint: `pop` on an empty array is already a no-op that returns `undefined`, so undoing past the start needs no special case - but appending that `undefined` would.

exam.prompt: A stack and a queue can both be implemented over the same array. Explain what actually distinguishes them, and why the restricted interface is a feature rather than a missing capability.
exam.explain: What distinguishes them is not the storage - both can be an array - but which end each operation is allowed to touch, and therefore the order in which items come back out. The restriction is the feature: because a stack exposes only one end, whole classes of bug become unwritable, and because neither structure permits access to the middle, every operation can be O(1). A deque removes the restriction and gains flexibility at exactly that cost - it is once again possible to read from the wrong end by mistake.

sections.title: Turning a key into an address
sections.body:
Every structure so far has made you **search** for things. An array can jump straight to a slot, but only if you already know the index. A hash table's whole idea is to **compute** the index from the key, so that finding a value costs the same as computing a small function - no search at all.

Two pieces do this. A **hash function** turns a key of any shape into an integer, and it must be deterministic: the same key must always produce the same number, or you would never find what you stored. Then that integer is squeezed into the table's range, almost always with `% buckets`, giving the **bucket index** - the actual slot.

A good hash function spreads keys evenly across the range, and changes a lot when the key changes a little. The polynomial hash below is the classic starting point: walk the characters, and at each step multiply the running value by a small prime and add the next character code. The multiplication is what makes position matter - without it `'ab'` and `'ba'` would collide, since addition does not care about order.

Be careful about what "O(1)" is claiming. Hashing a key is not free; it costs time proportional to the size of the **key**. The claim is that lookup does not get slower as the **table** grows, which is a different and much more useful promise.

annotations.text: The multiply-and-add is what makes position significant, so `'ab'` and `'ba'` land in different buckets. Taking the modulus every step, rather than only at the end, keeps `h` small enough to avoid overflowing into imprecise floating-point integers.
Two different keys landing in bucket 1. This is not a bug in the hash function - the next section shows why it is unavoidable.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the step that turns an arbitrary hash value into a legal bucket index for a table of `buckets` slots.
checkpoint.explain: The modulus is what guarantees the result is a legal index - it maps any integer into `0 .. buckets - 1`, which is exactly the range of the table. Dividing would give a fraction, and using the raw hash would index far off the end of the array.

sections.title: Collisions are not a bug
sections.body:
There are infinitely many possible keys and only `buckets` slots. By the **pigeonhole principle**, some pair of distinct keys must land in the same bucket - and not merely might, but **must**, for any hash function whatsoever. No amount of cleverness removes collisions. A hash table is therefore not "a mapping from keys to slots"; it is a mapping from keys to slots **plus a strategy for what to do when two keys want the same slot**.

The first strategy is **separate chaining**: each bucket holds a small list of entries, and a colliding key simply joins the list. Lookup hashes to the bucket, then scans that one short list comparing keys. If the hash spreads well and the table is not overloaded, those lists stay tiny - a handful of comparisons at most - which is where average O(1) comes from.

Notice the two comparisons that must both happen. The hash gets you to the right bucket, but the bucket may hold several keys, so you still have to compare the actual keys for equality. Skipping that second check is a classic bug: you find **a** value in the right bucket and return it, and it belongs to a different key entirely.

The worst case is unforgiving. If every key hashes to the same bucket - a bad hash function, or an adversary choosing keys deliberately - every operation degenerates to scanning one list of n entries, and the table becomes an O(n) linked list wearing a hash table's interface.

annotations.text: The key comparison inside the bucket. Without it, `set` would append a duplicate entry for a key already present, and `get` would return whichever collided entry happened to be first.
Two lookups, not one: hash to the bucket, then search within it. The second search is over a list you hope is one or two entries long - that hope is what the load factor manages.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: `'a'` and `'ab'` both hash to bucket 1, so that bucket's chain holds two keys while `'abc'` sits alone in bucket 2. Answering 1 assumes each key gets its own slot - which is precisely the assumption the pigeonhole principle forbids.

sections.title: Open addressing, and the trouble with deleting
sections.body:
The other strategy keeps everything in one flat array and never allocates a list. On a collision, **open addressing** simply looks elsewhere in the table for a free slot. The simplest rule is **linear probing**: if slot `i` is taken, try `i + 1`, then `i + 2`, wrapping around with `% size`. Lookup follows the identical path and stops at the first empty slot, because an empty slot proves the key was never inserted - had it been, it would have landed there.

This is faster than chaining in practice, because everything lives in contiguous memory and the processor's cache rewards that heavily. It costs you two things.

The first is **clustering**. Once a run of occupied slots forms, any key hashing anywhere into that run must walk to its end, and lands at the end - making the run longer. Long runs grow faster than short ones, so the damage compounds.

The second is deletion, which is genuinely subtle. You cannot simply empty a slot. If a key was displaced past that slot by probing, blanking the slot puts an empty cell in the middle of its probe path, and every future lookup for that key stops there and reports "not found" - even though the key is still sitting in the table. The fix is a **tombstone**: a marker meaning "empty now, but keep probing past me". Insertion may reuse a tombstone; lookup must walk through it.

annotations.text: The wrap is what makes the probe sequence a cycle over the whole table rather than a walk off the end of the array.
The `steps` counter is not decoration. Without a bound, a full table sends this loop around forever, because there is no empty slot to stop at.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `probeOrder(start, size)` returning the complete linear-probing sequence for a table of `size` slots beginning at index `start` - that is, every index it would visit, in order, before returning to where it began.
checkpoint.hint: Add an offset that runs from 0 up to `size - 1` and take the modulus each time, rather than incrementing and testing for the end of the array.
checkpoint.explain: Because the step is 1 and the table size bounds the walk, linear probing visits every slot exactly once before repeating - which is why insertion can only fail when the table is genuinely full. A probe step that shared a factor with `size` would revisit slots and could miss free ones entirely, which is why step sizes and table sizes are chosen with care.

sections.title: Load factor, and what may be used as a key
sections.body:
The **load factor** is the honest measure of how crowded a table is: entries divided by buckets. It is the number that decides whether the average-O(1) promise still holds. Under chaining, the load factor is the average chain length, so at 0.75 the typical lookup compares about one key. Under open addressing it is worse than linear - probe lengths climb sharply as the table approaches full, which is why open-addressed tables usually resize at a lower threshold.

When the load factor crosses the threshold the table **resizes**: allocate a larger array, usually double, and re-insert every existing entry. Re-insert, not copy - the bucket index is computed as `% buckets`, so changing the bucket count changes where every key belongs. A resize is O(n), but doubling means it happens rarely enough that the amortised cost per insert is still O(1), exactly the argument that justified the dynamic array's growth.

Finally, what may serve as a key. A key must satisfy two conditions, and the second is the one people forget. It must be hashable, and it must be **stable** - equal keys must hash equally, and a key must not change while it is in the table. Mutating an object after using it as a key strands the entry: the table looks in the bucket the new value hashes to, finds nothing, and the entry sits unreachable in its old bucket forever. This is why the usual advice is to key on immutable values.

One JavaScript trap deserves naming. A plain `{}` is not an empty dictionary - it inherits `toString`, `constructor` and friends, so `counts['constructor']` is a function rather than `undefined`. Use `new Map()`, or `Object.create(null)` for an object with no prototype.

annotations.text: Inherited from `Object.prototype`. Any counter written as `counts[w] = (counts[w] || 0) + 1` over a plain object produces nonsense for this key, because the inherited function is truthy.
`Object.create(null)` makes an object with no prototype at all, so the only keys it has are the ones you put there. `new Map()` is the better answer when keys are not strings.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `loadFactor(size, buckets)` returning the table's load factor - entries divided by buckets. A table with no buckets has a load factor of `0` rather than dividing by zero.
checkpoint.hint: Guard `buckets === 0` before dividing - in JavaScript `1 / 0` is `Infinity` rather than an error, so the bug would propagate silently instead of throwing.
checkpoint.explain: A load factor above 1 is perfectly legal under chaining - it just means the average bucket holds more than one entry - but it is impossible under open addressing, where each slot holds at most one. The zero-bucket guard matters because JavaScript returns `Infinity` rather than throwing, so an unguarded division would quietly poison every later comparison against the threshold.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: The first line is the determinism requirement: the same key must always hash the same, or nothing could ever be found again. The second shows different keys usually differing - but only usually, which is the whole reason collision handling exists.

guided-practice.prompt: Explain why no hash function, however well designed, can eliminate collisions entirely. Your answer should make clear that this is a counting argument rather than a shortcoming that better engineering could fix.
guided-practice.explain: It is a counting argument, not an engineering shortfall: there are more possible keys than there are buckets, so by the pigeonhole principle some pair of distinct keys must share a slot - and this holds for every hash function that has ever been or could be written. A better hash spreads keys more evenly and so makes collisions rarer and more uniform, which is worth a great deal in practice, but it cannot make them impossible. That is why a hash table is defined by its collision strategy as much as by its hash.

guided-practice.prompt: A table of 5 slots uses linear probing with `hash(k) = k % 5`, starting empty. Insert 5, then 10, then 7, then 15. Give the index each key lands in.
guided-practice.explain: 5, 10 and 15 all hash to 0, so they form a cluster running 0, 1, 3. The interesting one is 7: it hashes to 2, a slot nobody else wanted, yet it is caught in the cluster anyway - and by occupying 2 it forces 15 out to 3. That is clustering doing its damage: keys that never collided by hash still interfere by position.

guided-practice.prompt: Put the steps of a chained hash table's `get(key)` into the order they must happen.
fragments: compute the hash of the key
reduce the hash modulo the bucket count to get an index
look up the chain stored at that index
scan the chain comparing each entry's key for equality
return the matching entry's value, or null if the scan found nothing
guided-practice.explain: The step people leave out is the fourth. Reaching the right bucket is not the same as finding the right key, because the bucket may hold several - so a lookup that returns the first entry in the bucket returns another key's value whenever a collision has occurred.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the resize check that runs after each insertion.
guided-practice.explain: Growing by a constant multiple is what makes the amortised cost O(1); growing by a fixed number of buckets instead would make insertion O(n) on average, for the same reason a dynamic array doubles rather than adding one slot. `rehashEverything` is unavoidable because the bucket index depends on the bucket count, so every key belongs somewhere new.

guided-practice.prompt: In an open-addressed table, why can a deleted entry not simply be set back to empty? Describe the failure concretely and name the fix.
guided-practice.explain: Lookup stops at the first empty slot, because an empty slot proves the key was never inserted. So blanking a slot in the middle of some other key's probe path makes that key unreachable: the search halts at the hole and reports not-found while the entry sits two slots further on. A tombstone - a marker meaning 'empty, but keep going' - preserves the path. Lookup probes through tombstones; insertion may reuse them.

implementation.prompt: Write `hashString(s, buckets)` returning a bucket index for the string `s`. Use the polynomial hash from the lesson: start at 0, and for each character set `h = (h * 31 + charCode) % buckets`. The empty string hashes to 0.
implementation.hint: Take the modulus inside the loop, not once at the end - it keeps `h` small and the result is identical, because modular arithmetic distributes over multiplication and addition.
implementation.explain: A table of one bucket is the edge case worth keeping: every key hashes to 0, which is the degenerate hash table that behaves exactly like a list.
