annotations.text: Path halving - point each node at its grandparent while walking up. It flattens the tree almost as well as full path compression and needs no second pass or recursion.

The rank increases only when two trees of equal height merge. That is what keeps the height logarithmic, and it is why rank is an upper bound on height rather than an exact measure once compression has flattened things.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the loop that walks to an element's representative.
checkpoint.explain: The representative is defined as the element that is its own parent, so the walk continues exactly while that is not yet true. Any other stopping rule - a fixed number of steps, or a null parent - either stops early in the middle of a chain or never stops at all, since a representative's self-loop is what terminates the walk.

sections.title: Where connectivity questions actually come from
sections.body:
Union-Find looks abstract until you notice how many problems are connectivity questions wearing other clothes.

**Cycle detection in an undirected graph.** Process the edges one at a time. For edge `(a, b)`, if `find(a)` already equals `find(b)` then a path between them existed before this edge, so this edge closes a cycle. Otherwise union them. One pass, no traversal, no visited set.

**Kruskal's minimum spanning tree.** Sort the edges by weight and add each one unless it would form a cycle - which is the test above. Union-Find is what makes Kruskal practical; without it, checking each candidate edge for a cycle would need a graph search.

**Counting connected components.** Start with n components and decrement each time a union actually merges two distinct sets. That is what the boolean return from `union` is for: it distinguishes a real merge from a statement you already knew.

**Percolation, image segmentation, network reachability, type unification** - all the same shape. The recognisable signature is: things merge, never split, and you only ever ask whether two are together.

The honest limitation is worth repeating, because it decides whether the structure fits. Union-Find cannot undo a union, cannot enumerate a set's members without scanning everything, and cannot answer **how** two elements are connected - only that they are. When you need the path, you need a graph traversal, not this.

annotations.text: The boolean is doing real work. A duplicate edge, or one between vertices already connected by another route, must not reduce the count - so `union` reporting whether it actually merged anything is what keeps this correct.
The same boolean, read the other way round. A union that changes nothing means the two endpoints were already connected, so this edge is the one that closes a cycle.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `countComponents(n, edges)` returning how many connected components exist among vertices `0` to `n - 1` given the list of undirected `edges`, each `[a, b]`. Duplicate edges and self-loops must not change the count.
checkpoint.hint: Decrement only when the two representatives actually differ - that single check handles duplicate edges and self-loops without any special case for either.
checkpoint.explain: Tests 3 and 5 are the whole point. A repeated edge and a self-loop both produce two equal representatives, so the merge check rejects them automatically and no special-casing is needed. Decrementing on every edge instead would report 0 components for test 3 and 2 for test 5 - both nonsense, and both invisible on the simple test 2.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Only the final node of the inserted word is marked. Every node along the way exists - the path `ca` is real - but existing and being a stored word are different claims, which is exactly what the flag separates.

guided-practice.prompt: A trie holds `car`, `card` and `cat`. Give the number of children each node has, walking down from the root along `c`, then `a`, then `r`.
guided-practice.explain: The branching happens exactly where the words stop agreeing: `ca` is shared by all three, then `r` and `t` split off, and `card` extends `car` by one more child. Three words of three and four letters cost six nodes instead of ten, and that saving is the whole economic case for a trie.

guided-practice.prompt: A colleague proposes replacing an autocomplete trie with a hash set of the same words, arguing that hash lookup is O(1) and therefore faster. Explain what breaks.
guided-practice.explain: Autocomplete never asks the question a hash set answers. It asks for every word starting with a prefix, and hashing deliberately scatters similar keys into unrelated buckets - so `ca` tells you nothing about where `cat` is stored, and the only way to find the matches is to examine every key in the set. In a trie the prefix is a node and the answers are its subtree, so the cost is proportional to the number of matches rather than the size of the dictionary. The O(1) claim is also about the wrong operation: both structures must look at the whole key, so exact lookup is comparable, and the difference is entirely in what else each can answer.

guided-practice.prompt: Six elements 0 to 5, each its own set. Apply `union(0,1)`, then `union(2,3)`, then `union(1,2)`, then `union(4,5)`. After each, give the number of disjoint sets remaining.
guided-practice.explain: Each successful union reduces the count by exactly one, because it replaces two sets with one. The third is the interesting one: 1 and 2 are in different sets already containing 0 and 3, so a single union merges four elements at once - the operation is on representatives, not on elements, which is why it costs the same regardless of set size.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the union-by-rank tie-break, taken when both trees have equal rank.
guided-practice.explain: Attaching a tree under a root of equal rank is the only case that makes the result taller, so it is the only case that increments. Incrementing on every union would inflate the rank until it stopped reflecting height and the balancing decisions became arbitrary.

guided-practice.prompt: Put the steps of detecting a cycle in an undirected graph with Union-Find into the order they must happen.
fragments: put every vertex in its own set
take the next edge (a, b)
find the representative of a and the representative of b
if the two representatives are equal, report a cycle
otherwise union the two sets and continue
guided-practice.explain: The equality test must come before the union, not after - once the sets are merged the representatives are equal regardless, so the evidence of a cycle is destroyed by the very operation that follows it. This is the whole of Kruskal's cycle check, and it needs no graph traversal or visited set at all.

implementation.prompt: Write `startingWith(words, prefix)` returning every stored word beginning with `prefix`, in lexicographic order, by building a trie and collecting the subtree at the prefix. A word that equals the prefix counts. An empty prefix returns every word.
implementation.hint: Check the terminal flag before descending, so a word equal to the prefix comes out first, and sort the child keys to get lexicographic order for free.
implementation.explain: Test 2 is the case people miss: `car` is both the prefix and a stored word, so it must appear in its own results. Test 4 shows the trie sorting for nothing - visiting children in sorted key order makes the whole traversal lexicographic, which a hash set could only match by sorting afterwards.

implementation.prompt: Write `countPrefixNodes(words)` returning how many nodes a trie holding all of `words` contains, **excluding** the root. This is the number of distinct prefixes across the whole word list.
implementation.hint: Count only when you actually create a node. Counting every character instead measures the total length of the words, which is what the trie exists to beat.
implementation.explain: `car` and `cart` are seven characters and cost four nodes, because `car` is entirely shared; `car` and `dog` are six characters and cost six, because they share nothing. That gap is the trie's whole economics - it rewards dense overlapping key sets and punishes long unrelated ones, which is why it suits dictionaries and URL paths and suits random identifiers badly.

implementation.prompt: Write `longestCommonPrefix(words)` returning the longest prefix shared by every word. Build a trie and walk down from the root while there is exactly one child and no word has ended. Return `''` when there is no common prefix or the list is empty.
implementation.hint: Two things stop the descent: the path branching, and a word ending here. Missing the second walks past a word that is itself the answer.
implementation.explain: Test 5 is why the terminal check matters. After `ab` the trie has one child `c`, so a descent that only watches for branching keeps going and returns `abc` - a string that is not a prefix of `ab` at all. A word ending is as much a stopping condition as a fork, and forgetting it is invisible until one word is a prefix of another.

implementation.prompt: Write `unionFindOps(n, ops)` over elements `0` to `n - 1`. `ops` is an array of strings: `'union A B'` merges two sets, `'same A B'` asks whether two elements are in the same set. Return an array of the booleans produced by the `'same'` operations.
implementation.hint: Never compare the elements themselves - always compare their representatives, because two elements in the same set almost never point at each other directly.
implementation.explain: Test 3 is transitivity emerging from the structure rather than being programmed: 0 and 3 are unrelated until `union(1,2)` joins the two pairs, after which one `find` from each end reaches the same representative. Test 4 is the reflexive case - an element is always in its own set - which falls out for free because `find(0)` equals `find(0)` without any special case.

implementation.prompt: Write `hasCycle(n, edges)` returning `true` if the undirected graph on vertices `0` to `n - 1` contains a cycle. Use Union-Find rather than a traversal. A self-loop is a cycle, and a repeated edge between the same two vertices is also a cycle.
implementation.hint: Test the two representatives for equality before merging them - after the union they are equal no matter what, so the evidence is gone.
implementation.explain: Tests 4 and 5 both fall out of the same check with no special handling: a self-loop has one vertex whose representative trivially equals itself, and a repeated edge finds the two endpoints already merged by the first copy. This is Kruskal's cycle test in full, and it is why Kruskal is practical - checking each candidate edge with a graph search instead would cost O(V + E) every time.

implementation.prompt: This Union-Find compares the elements' parents instead of their representatives, so it gets transitive cases wrong. Fix it, keeping the name `sameSet`. It takes `n` and an array of ops as in the previous challenges, and returns the booleans from the `'same'` operations.
implementation.hint: One step up the chain is not enough - membership is decided by where the whole walk ends, and unions must link representatives rather than raw elements.
implementation.explain: Looking one level up works only while every chain is one link long, so the bug survives test 1 and dies on test 2, where 0 and 2 are in the same set through 1 but have different immediate parents. Test 5 makes it worse by building a chain of four. Two things must change: `find` has to walk to the representative, and `union` has to link representatives rather than elements - linking `b` directly under `a` can otherwise detach an entire subtree from the set it was already in.

exam.prompt: Why does a trie node need a terminal marker?
choices: Because a node's existence only proves some word passes through it, not that the path so far is a word
Because leaves cannot store characters
Because it records how many words share the prefix
Because it marks where the alphabet ends
exam.explain: Storing `cart` creates nodes for `c`, `ca` and `car`, none of which is a stored word. Without the flag the trie reports every prefix of every word as stored - and note the flag is not the same as being a leaf, since `car` can be a word with `card` continuing below it.

exam.prompt: Which of these can a trie do that a hash set of the same strings cannot? Select all that apply.
choices: List every stored word beginning with a given prefix without examining unrelated words
Produce its contents in lexicographic order without a separate sort
Find the longest prefix shared by all stored words by descending from the root
Report whether an exact string is stored
exam.explain: The first three all exploit the fact that a trie's structure mirrors the keys' shared structure. Exact membership is the one thing both do comparably - each must look at the whole key - which is why quoting O(1) for the hash set misses the point: the difference is in the questions the trie can answer at all.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: `find(2)` walks 2 to 1 to 0 and reports the representative correctly, but this version does no compression, so `parent[2]` is still 1 and the next walk costs the same again. Path compression is exactly the missing step: point every node on the walk directly at the representative so the second lookup is one hop.

exam.prompt: Complete the descent that collects every word under a prefix node.
exam.explain: The flag is checked before descending so that a word equal to the prefix is reported first, and sorting the child keys makes the entire traversal lexicographic without any sort at the end. Object key order is insertion order for string keys, which is not alphabetical, so the sort is doing real work.

exam.prompt: Put the steps of Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm into the order they must happen.
fragments: put every vertex in its own disjoint set
sort all the edges by weight, lightest first
take the next lightest edge
if its endpoints are already in the same set, discard it as a cycle
otherwise union the sets and add the edge to the tree
exam.explain: The sort is what makes the greedy choice correct, and Union-Find is what makes the cycle test cheap enough for the greed to be practical - without it each candidate edge would need a graph search to decide whether it closes a cycle. Adding the edge before testing would build the cycle you are trying to avoid.

exam.prompt: Five elements 0 to 4, each its own set, using union by rank with ties linking the second argument under the first. Apply `union(0,1)`, `union(2,3)`, `union(0,2)`. Give the rank of element 0 after each.
exam.explain: Rank rises only when two trees of equal rank merge. The first union joins two rank-0 elements and lifts 0 to rank 1; the second does not touch 0 at all; the third merges two rank-1 trees and lifts it to 2. Three unions and a rank of 2 for four elements is the logarithmic growth that keeps `find` short.

exam.prompt: Give the time complexity of looking a word of length m up in a trie holding n words, and explain what is notable about it compared with a hash table.
exam.explain: One step per character, so O(m) in the key length and completely independent of n - the trie can hold ten words or ten million and the lookup costs the same. A hash table is also about O(m), since it must hash the whole key, but its guarantee is weaker: it is an average that assumes a well-behaved hash and a bounded load factor, it has a worst case of O(n) when keys collide, and it needs periodic O(n) resizes. The trie has no load factor, no resize, and no adversarial input - which is worth more than it first appears.

exam.prompt: Write `wordBreakable(dict, text)` returning `true` if `text` can be split into a sequence of one or more words all present in `dict`. Use a trie so that each attempted split walks characters rather than re-testing whole substrings. The empty text is not breakable.
exam.hint: Walking the trie from a position gives you every dictionary word starting there in one pass. Memoise by position, or the same suffix is re-solved exponentially often.
exam.explain: The trie turns 'which dictionary words start here?' into a single forward walk that stops the moment no word can continue - test 2 abandons `catf` after four characters instead of testing every substring. Test 1 needs the backtracking: `cats` is a word and leads nowhere, so the split at `cat` has to be tried too. The memo is what keeps this polynomial rather than exponential, since without it every failed split re-solves the same suffix.

exam.prompt: Union-Find answers connectivity questions in near-constant time. Name two questions about connectivity it deliberately cannot answer, and explain what you would use instead.
exam.explain: It cannot tell you **how** two elements are connected - only that they are - because it stores a representative rather than any route, so a shortest or actual path needs a graph traversal such as BFS or DFS. It also cannot undo a union or split a set, since merging is one-way, and it cannot enumerate a set's members without scanning every element and calling find on each. That narrowness is the point: answering exactly one question is what allows the near-constant amortised bound that path compression and union by rank deliver. When you need paths, membership lists, or removal, you need an adjacency structure and a traversal instead.

sections.title: Read the Access Pattern First
sections.body:
A structure is never chosen because it is elegant. It is chosen because the operation you perform a million times a second is the one it makes cheap, and the operation it makes expensive is one you almost never perform.

So the design starts by writing the **access pattern** down: which operations, at what frequency, in what ratio of reads to writes. An array gives $O(1)$ indexed reads and $O(n)$ membership tests; a hash set inverts both, at the price of losing order and of storing buckets it never fills. Neither is better - they are answers to different questions.

The run below asks the same four membership questions two ways. The array pays a scan per question because it has no idea where anything lives; the set pays one hash per question, because that is precisely what it bought with its extra memory.

annotations.text: The scan is the whole cost. Nothing about an array narrows the search, so a query near the end always costs close to the full length.
Building the set is one O(n) pass and extra memory - a fixed price paid once so that every later question costs O(1).
Four lookups, four hashes, no matter how large data grew. That flatness is the thing being bought.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `dedupePreserveOrder(items)`: return a new array holding each distinct value of `items` exactly once, in the order of its first appearance. Choose the structure that makes the repeated question cheap. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: The output array preserves order and the set answers 'have I seen this?' - two structures because there are two questions. Calling `out.indexOf(x)` instead is the tempting single-structure answer, and it turns an O(n) pass into O(n^2) by re-scanning everything already emitted.

sections.title: When No Single Structure Will Do
sections.body:
Some access patterns name two operations that no one structure makes cheap at once. Fast lookup by key wants a hash map, which has no notion of order; cheap removal from an arbitrary position wants a linked list, which has no notion of lookup.

The answer is **composition**: run both over the same keys and let each one answer what it is good at. A hash map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list of those nodes, gives $O(1)$ find **and** $O(1)$ unlink - because the map hands you the node directly, and that node's `prev` and `next` pointers let it leave the list without anyone walking it.

The cost is real and worth naming: two structures over the same keys means roughly twice the bookkeeping memory, and every mutation must update both or they drift apart. Consistency across the pair becomes your invariant, not the language's.

The list below stores its links as two flat maps, `nextOf` and `prevOf`, so it can be printed and reasoned about without chasing object references.

annotations.text: Both neighbours are known in O(1). This single line is what the prev pointer exists to make possible.
A null predecessor means the key was the head, so the head moves rather than some next pointer being rewritten.
Unlink then push front is a move-to-front in O(1), with no traversal anywhere - the property the LRU cache is built on.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `unlinkKey(nextOf, prevOf, key)`. `nextOf` maps each key to its successor (`null` at the tail) and `prevOf` maps each key to its predecessor (`null` at the head). Return a **new** successor map with `key` removed and its neighbours joined; if `key` is not in the list, return an unchanged copy. Do not mutate the arguments. Nothing is given to you.

tests.input: {A: 'B', B: 'C', C: null}, {A: null, B: 'A', C: 'B'}, 'B'
{A: 'B', B: 'C', C: null}, {A: null, B: 'A', C: 'B'}, 'A'
{A: 'B', B: 'C', C: null}, {A: null, B: 'A', C: 'B'}, 'C'

checkpoint.explain: Removing the head is the case that separates a real answer from a sketch: there is no predecessor to repoint, so the only correct action is to leave every remaining entry alone. The tempting bug is writing `out[prevOf[key]] = nextOf[key]` unconditionally, which invents an entry under the key `null` whenever the head is removed.

sections.title: The LRU Cache, Assembled
sections.body:
An **LRU cache** holds at most `capacity` entries and, when it overflows, discards the one least recently used. Its access pattern is exactly the pair from the last section: look a key up by name, and move or remove an entry sitting at an arbitrary position in a recency order.

So it is built as a hash map from key to list node plus a doubly linked list ordered most-recent-first. `get` hashes to the node, unlinks it and pushes it to the front: $O(1)$. `put` does the same and, if the size now exceeds capacity, drops the tail - which the list already points at, so eviction is $O(1)$ rather than a search for the oldest.

JavaScript's `Map` iterates in insertion order, which is itself a hash table with a linked list threaded through it, so `delete` then `set` re-seats a key at the back and `map.keys().next().value` is the oldest key. In a language whose hash table gives no such guarantee you build the pair by hand, exactly as above.

annotations.text: Delete then set is the move-to-front. A read mutates the structure, which is why an LRU cache is never safe to share without a lock.
Overwriting an existing key must re-seat it, not leave it where it was, or a hot key can be evicted while it is still in use.
The oldest key is the front of the iteration order - the list tail. Finding it costs nothing, which is the whole reason for keeping the order.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `recencyOrder(accesses)`: given an array of keys in the order they were touched, return the distinct keys ordered most recently used first. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: Recency is defined by the **last** touch, not the first, so the array has to be read backwards; walking forwards keeping first appearances and reversing gives `['c','b','a']` for the first case instead of `['c','a','b']`. That asymmetry is exactly what the cache encodes by moving a key to the front on every hit rather than only on insertion.

sections.title: Turning an Index Inside Out
sections.body:
A corpus is naturally stored **forward**: document id to the list of terms it contains. Ask that structure 'which documents contain **kite**?' and there is no answer but to open every document, so the query costs $\Theta(D)$ in the number of documents however rare the word is.

**Inverting** the index stores the transpose: term to the sorted list of document ids containing it, its **posting list**. The query becomes one hash lookup and a read of exactly the documents that match. An AND of two terms walks both posting lists in sorted order, advancing whichever holds the smaller id, for $O(p+q)$ in the two lengths - the same merge step merge sort uses.

The price is paid on the other side. The index holds one posting per distinct term-document pair, so its size is proportional to the total distinct term occurrences, and every new or edited document must touch one posting list per distinct term it contains. This is the archetypal **read-optimised** structure: a bargain for a corpus queried far more often than it is written, and a liability for one rewritten constantly.

annotations.text: The Set collapses repeats within one document: a posting records that a term occurs, not how often, so a word used twice earns one entry.
Sorting the posting lists is what makes queries cheap later - the merge below depends on it and would otherwise need a fresh hash set per query.
Advance only the side holding the smaller id. Neither list is ever restarted, so the whole intersection costs one pass over each.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `invertDocs(docs)`: `docs` is an object mapping a document id string to an array of terms. Return an object mapping each term to the array of document ids containing it, each list sorted ascending as strings and free of repeats. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: Two things are easy to skip and both are load-bearing: de-duplicating terms within a document, so a repeated word does not push the same id twice, and sorting each posting list, which is what lets later queries merge two lists in a single pass instead of building a hash set every time.

compose-the-structure.prompt: Design `lruRun(capacity, ops)`. `ops` is an array of operations: `['put', key, value]` stores a value, `['get', key]` reads one. The cache holds at most `capacity` entries and evicts the least recently used when it overflows; both `get` and `put` count as a use, and re-putting an existing key updates it and counts as a use. Return an array holding the result of each `get` in order - the stored value, or `null` if the key is not cached. Nothing is given to you.
compose-the-structure.explain: The first case turns on `get('a')` promoting `a`, so the eviction that follows takes `b` and not `a`; a design that reorders only on `put` returns `[1, 2, null, 3]` and looks entirely plausible. The last case punishes the other common slip - re-putting `a` without re-seating it leaves `a` at the old end of the order, so it survives when it should have been the entry evicted.

compose-the-structure.prompt: Design `buildIndex(docs)`. `docs` is an array of `[docId, terms]` pairs where `docId` is a number and `terms` is an array of strings. Return an object mapping each term to the ascending-sorted array of distinct document ids containing it. Nothing is given to you.
compose-the-structure.explain: The last case catches an implementation that assumes documents arrive in id order: they may arrive in any order, and a posting list is only useful sorted, so the sort is part of the contract rather than a tidy-up. Note too that JavaScript's default `sort` compares as strings, which would put 10 before 2 - numeric ids need an explicit comparator.

compose-the-structure.prompt: Design `searchAll(index, terms)`. `index` maps each term to an ascending-sorted array of document ids. Return the ascending-sorted array of ids containing **every** term in `terms`. A term absent from the index matches nothing. Return `[]` when `terms` is empty. Nothing is given to you.
compose-the-structure.explain: An empty `terms` list is the case worth arguing about: strictly, every document contains all of no terms, but a search box that returns the whole corpus for an empty query is a bug, so the contract fixes it at `[]`. The missing-term case must also collapse the result to nothing rather than being skipped, or `['red','yellow']` wrongly returns everything red.

compose-the-structure.prompt: Design `minStackRun(ops)`. `ops` is an array of `['push', n]`, `['pop']` and `['min']` operations on a stack of numbers. Return an array holding the answer to each `['min']` in order - the smallest value currently on the stack, or `null` when it is empty. Every operation must cost $O(1)$; scanning the stack on each `min` is not acceptable. `pop` on an empty stack is a no-op. Nothing is given to you.
compose-the-structure.explain: The composition is a second stack recording the minimum **as of** each push, so a pop restores the previous minimum for free - $O(n)$ extra space bought $O(1)$ queries. Pushing 2 twice is the case that kills the thriftier variant that records a value only when it strictly improves the minimum: after one pop its bookkeeping stack is empty while the data stack still holds a 2.

compose-the-structure.prompt: Design `topKFrequent(items, k)`: return the `k` most frequently occurring values in `items`, most frequent first, breaking ties towards the value that appears earliest in `items`. Return every distinct value if `k` exceeds how many there are. Nothing is given to you.
compose-the-structure.explain: Counting needs a hash map because the question asked of every item is 'how many so far', and the ordering needs something the map cannot supply, so the two are composed. The `['x','y','y','x','z']` case is the tie-break: both reach 2, and only a recorded first-appearance index - not the map's iteration order, which you should never rely on across languages - resolves it deterministically.

defend-the-choice.prompt: State the worst-case cost of a single `get` and a single `put` on an LRU cache built as a hash map from key to node plus a doubly linked list in recency order. Justify it by naming what each half of the composition contributes, eviction included.
defend-the-choice.explain: The hash map turns a key into a node with no search, and holding the node means its `prev` and `next` let it be unlinked and re-inserted at the head without walking anything; eviction takes the list's tail, which is already known. The tempting wrong answer is linear time for eviction, which is what you would pay if the map alone stored timestamps and the oldest entry had to be found by scanning every one of them.

defend-the-choice.prompt: A colleague proposes replacing the doubly linked list in the LRU cache with a singly linked list, to save one pointer per entry. Explain precisely what breaks, and say what that extra pointer was buying.
defend-the-choice.explain: Removing a node means rewriting its predecessor's `next` pointer, and a singly linked list can only find a predecessor by walking from the head - so every cache hit degrades from constant to linear time and the hash map's instant lookup is wasted. The saving is one machine word per entry, set against a linear factor on the hottest operation in the structure, which is the shape of trade that space almost always wins.

defend-the-choice.prompt: Two terms have posting lists of lengths $p$ and $q$, each an ascending-sorted array of document ids. Give the cost of answering the AND of the two terms, and justify why a single pass over each list suffices.
defend-the-choice.explain: Because both lists are sorted, comparing the two front elements and advancing whichever holds the smaller id can never skip a match, so each index moves forward at most once per element and the whole intersection is one merge pass. The tempting answer is $O(pq)$, which is what you pay by checking each id of one list against all of the other - correct, and needlessly quadratic given the ordering the index already maintains for free.

defend-the-choice.prompt: A service must answer one question: has user `u` been seen today? Ten million distinct users are recorded per day, and a thousand membership queries arrive per second. Choose a structure, and defend it specifically against a sorted array searched by binary search.
defend-the-choice.explain: A hash set wins because the workload is insert-heavy: binary search makes the query logarithmic, which is perfectly fine, but keeping the array sorted costs $O(n)$ element moves per insertion, and ten million of those is quadratic work no query saving can repay. The defence has to be about the insert path - answering only that hash lookup beats binary search picks the right structure for the wrong reason, since at ten million entries $\log_2 n$ is about 23, a constant that decides nothing on its own.

defend-the-choice.prompt: State the space and write-time price of maintaining an inverted index over a corpus, and say exactly which query cost it removes. Then describe a workload on which paying that price would be a mistake.
defend-the-choice.explain: The index stores one posting per distinct term-document pair, so it can rival the text it describes in size, and every write must touch one posting list per distinct term in the changed document; in exchange, a term query stops being a $\Theta(D)$ scan over every document and becomes a hash lookup plus a read of only the matching ids. It is a mistake wherever writes outnumber reads, or the corpus is small enough that the scan was already fast - a per-user notes store rewritten constantly and searched rarely pays the whole price and collects almost none of the benefit.

exam.prompt: Design `lruEvictions(capacity, keys)`: each entry of `keys` is an access, which inserts the key if it is absent and marks it most recently used either way. Return the array of keys evicted, in the order they were evicted. Nothing is given to you.
exam.explain: The first case is deliberately circular: `a` is evicted, then accessed again and re-inserted, which costs `b`, whose slot then costs `c`. A design that treats an evicted key as permanently gone, or that fails to promote on a repeat access, diverges here; the capacity-1 case with a repeated key checks that a re-access is not mistaken for an insertion that overflows.

exam.prompt: You compute the $k$ most frequent of $n$ items by counting into a hash map and then placing each distinct value into a bucket indexed by its count, reading the buckets from the highest downwards. Give the total cost in $n$ and justify why no sort appears in it.
exam.explain: Counting is one pass, there are at most $n$ distinct values and no count exceeds $n$, so an array of $n+1$ buckets holds everything and sweeping it downwards is another pass - three linear passes, hence $O(n)$. The comparison sort disappears because the sort key is a small bounded integer used directly as an index; the price is the $O(n)$ bucket array, most of which is typically empty.

exam.prompt: A job queue takes thousands of appends per second at one end and removals from the other end by a single consumer. Nothing else is ever asked of it. Choose between a growable array with head and tail indices and a doubly linked list of heap-allocated nodes, and defend the winner.
exam.explain: Both give $O(1)$ per operation on paper, so the asymptotics decide nothing and the constants decide everything: the array stores elements contiguously with no per-element allocation and no pointer overhead, while the linked list allocates and frees a node per job and scatters them across memory, defeating the prefetcher. The array's cost is amortised resizing, which a ring buffer removes entirely, and it is the wrong choice only when elements must be removed from the middle - which this access pattern never does.

exam.prompt: In an LRU cache built from a hash map plus a linked list, why must the list be doubly linked?
choices: A singly linked list cannot be traversed from head to tail
Unlinking a node on a cache hit needs its predecessor, which a singly linked list can only find by walking from the head
The hash map cannot store a reference to a node in a singly linked list
Eviction needs the last node, and a singly linked list cannot keep a tail pointer
exam.explain: Everything the cache does on a hit ends in a removal from the middle of the order, and removal rewrites the predecessor's `next` pointer, so the predecessor must be reachable in constant time. The last option is the tempting one - a singly linked list keeps a tail pointer perfectly well for appends; what it cannot do is find the node **before** an arbitrary node.

exam.prompt: Put the steps of a successful `get` on a hash-map-plus-doubly-linked-list LRU cache into the order they must happen.
fragments: hash the key to find its node in the map, in O(1)
rewrite the node's neighbours' pointers so it leaves the list
splice the node back in immediately after the head
return the value stored on the node
exam.explain: The map lookup must come first because every later step needs the node it yields, and the unlink must precede the re-insertion because splicing a node that is still linked in its old position corrupts the list. Note the map itself is never rewritten - the key still points at the same node, only the node's position changed, which is why a hit costs no hashing beyond that first step.

exam.prompt: Design `searchAny(index, terms)`. `index` maps each term to an ascending-sorted array of document ids. Return the ascending-sorted array of ids containing **at least one** of `terms`, with no repeats. A term absent from the index contributes nothing, and an empty `terms` gives `[]`. Nothing is given to you.
exam.explain: An OR query is a union, so the structure that matters is the set suppressing a document that appears under two different terms - concatenating the posting lists returns `2` twice in the first case. The last test forces the output sort to be genuine rather than inherited: that posting list arrives unsorted, and the contract promises the caller ascending order regardless of what the index contained.

exam.prompt: Select every true statement about an inverted index over a corpus of documents.
choices: Its size is roughly proportional to the number of distinct term-document pairs in the corpus
An AND of two posting lists of lengths p and q can be answered in O(p + q) because both are kept sorted
It makes adding a new document cheaper than the forward document-to-terms map does
It answers 'which terms does document 7 contain?' faster than the forward map does
It trades extra space and write cost for a term query that no longer scans every document
exam.explain: The two false options describe the direction the index gave up: a write must now touch one posting list per distinct term instead of appending a single record, and the document-to-terms question is precisely what the forward map answers in one lookup. Inverting is a transpose, so whatever becomes cheap in one direction becomes expensive in the other.

exam.prompt: Complete the body of `put` for a `Map`-backed LRU cache, so that overwriting an existing key also re-seats it as most recently used.
exam.explain: `map.set` on a key already present updates the value but leaves the key where it was in the iteration order, so without the preceding `delete` a hot key that is written repeatedly still ages out and gets evicted. Deleting and re-setting is the `Map` equivalent of unlink-then-push-front on the doubly linked list.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: Reading `a` moves it behind `b`, so when `c` arrives the oldest key is `b` and it is `b` that disappears - the third line would read `b,c` and `b` would have survived if a read did not count as a use. That one mutation on the read path is the entire difference between LRU and first-in-first-out eviction.

exam.prompt: Trace the sorted-merge AND query over the posting lists `x = [1, 4, 7, 9]` and `y = [2, 4, 9]`. The algorithm compares `x[i]` with `y[j]`, emits on equality and advances both, and otherwise advances the index holding the smaller id. Write a pair as `a, b` and a list as comma-separated ids.

steps.label: which index advances after that first comparison, i or j
the pair compared immediately after that emission

exam.explain: Neither index ever moves backwards, which is why the pass is $O(p+q)$ rather than $O(pq)$: `1` and `2` are each discarded permanently the moment a larger id appears on the other side. Watch the emission at `4` - both indices advance, because a document already matched cannot match again, and advancing only one would compare `4` against `9` and stall.

sections.title: No Single Shape Answers Two Questions
sections.body:
A working system almost never rests on one structure, because a structure is an answer to **one** question asked cheaply, and everything else it does it does badly. A plain array of jobs answers **give me the job called `deploy`** in $O(n)$ and **give me the most urgent job** in $O(n)$ as well - both by walking the whole thing.

Add a second question and the array does not degrade gracefully; it simply scans again. Keeping the array sorted by priority makes the second question $O(1)$ and the first still $O(n)$, and now every insertion costs $O(n)$ to shift the elements after it.

The way out is not a cleverer array. It is **composition**: one structure per question, all of them describing the same jobs, all of them maintained on every write. You pay in bookkeeping - the update paths get longer and the structures can disagree - and you buy the ability to answer everything in logarithmic time or better.

The rest of this floor builds the three shapes your Trial needs, and then hands you the specification.

annotations.text: Lookup by id: a linear scan, because nothing in the array records where an id lives.
Smallest priority: a second linear scan over exactly the same elements, answering a different question.
Three jobs hides the cost. At a million jobs each question is a million reads - and that is per call, not once.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `bestByPriority(jobs)`: `jobs` is an array of `{ id, priority }` objects where a **smaller** priority is more urgent. Return the `id` of the most urgent job, breaking ties towards the earlier position in the array, or `null` for an empty array. This is the linear baseline a heap will replace. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: The strict `<` is what makes an earlier job win a tie; `<=` would silently prefer the last one, which is the sort of detail that turns a deterministic scheduler into a flaky one. Note the cost too: every call reads every job, so asking this question a thousand times over a thousand jobs is a million reads that a heap reduces to a few thousand.

sections.title: A Heap Keeps Only The Next Answer
sections.body:
A **binary min-heap** is a complete binary tree flattened into an array: the children of index $i$ sit at $2i+1$ and $2i+2$, so no pointers are stored at all. Its single invariant is that every node is no larger than its children, which puts the smallest element at index $0$ and says nothing whatsoever about the order of the rest.

That weak invariant is exactly why it is cheap. Pushing appends and **sifts up**, swapping with the parent while the parent is larger; popping moves the last element to the root and **sifts down**, swapping with the smaller child while that child is smaller. Each walks one root-to-leaf path, and a complete tree of $n$ nodes has height $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$, so both cost $O(\log n)$ while reading the minimum costs $O(1)$.

What a heap will not do is find an arbitrary element. There is no index and no ordering to binary-search, so locating a given value means scanning all $n$ slots - which is the awkward fact the next section is about.

annotations.text: Sift up stops the moment the parent is no larger; the invariant only ever concerned this one path.
Popping promotes the last element, not the second smallest - which is why the new root must then sift down.
Swap with the SMALLER child. Swapping with the larger one restores nothing and quietly corrupts the heap.
Prints [1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8]: ordered at the root and nowhere else. A heap is not a sorted array.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `heapPush(heap, value)`: `heap` is an array of numbers already satisfying the min-heap invariant. Append `value`, sift it up until its parent is no larger, and return the resulting array. Do not sort. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: Sifting up compares only against the parent chain, so a value belonging near the root climbs $\log n$ levels while one belonging at the bottom stops immediately. The `[1,3,2], 0` case catches a single-swap attempt: the new value has to keep climbing past 3 all the way to the root rather than stopping after one exchange.

sections.title: Cancelled Is Not The Same As Removed
sections.body:
Jobs get cancelled, and a heap has no way to delete one by name - finding it is precisely the $O(n)$ scan the heap was chosen to avoid. The standard answer is **lazy deletion**: record the cancellation somewhere that **can** be searched cheaply, leave the heap entry where it is, and discard it when it surfaces at the top.

That somewhere is a **hash index**, a map from job id to its record, giving $O(1)$ average lookup, insertion and deletion. The heap now holds entries that may be stale and the index is the authority on which are real, so the heap's size is an upper bound on the number of live jobs and never the count itself.

The cost is amortised rather than removed. Each entry is pushed once and discarded at most once, so $m$ operations still cost $O(m \log n)$ in total, even though a single `run` may throw away many corpses before it finds a live job. What you give up is a tight bound on any **individual** call, and a memory footprint that tracks cancellations rather than outstanding work.

annotations.text: The index is the authority. Cancelling writes here in O(1) and never touches the heap at all.
A stale entry is discarded at the moment it reaches the front, and only then - this is the lazy part.
Prints 3 and 2: the structure is holding one more entry than there are jobs left to run.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `nextLive(queue, cancelled)`: `queue` is an array of job ids in the order a heap would surface them, and `cancelled` is an array of ids that have been cancelled. Return `{ id, discarded }` - the first id in `queue` that is not cancelled, and how many stale entries were thrown away before reaching it. When every entry is stale, return `id` as `null` with `discarded` counting them all. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: Building a lookup from `cancelled` before the loop is the whole exercise: testing membership with `indexOf` inside the loop makes the scan quadratic and reintroduces exactly the linear search lazy deletion exists to avoid. The all-stale case matters because it is the only one where the caller must tell an empty queue apart from a queue full of corpses.

sections.title: Recency Is A List; Lookup Is Still A Map
sections.body:
The last shape records what ran recently, most recent first, keeping at most `capacity` entries. Held in an array, promoting an id to the front costs $O(n)$ because every element before it shifts - and that sits on the hot path of every single run.

A **doubly linked list** makes it $O(1)$: unlinking a node needs only its two neighbours, and both are one pointer away. On its own the list still cannot find the node for a given id without walking it, so it is paired with a hash index from id to node - the map finds the node, the list moves it. That pairing is the classic **LRU** structure, and both halves are load-bearing.

Eviction falls out of the same shape. Once the list is over `capacity` the least recently used entry is the tail, already located, so dropping it is one unlink and one key deletion with no search. Note that a repeat visit must **move** the existing node rather than insert a second one; a duplicate would leave the map pointing at a node the list has forgotten.

annotations.text: Unlinking touches only the neighbours - no shifting, no search. This is what the array could not do.
An id already present is detached and re-linked at the front: size is unchanged and no duplicate appears.
Over capacity: the tail is by construction the least recently used, so eviction needs no scan.
Watch 'a' return - it moves to the front and 'b' becomes the tail, so the next insert evicts b rather than a.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `touch(history, id, capacity)`: `history` is an array of ids, most recently used first, holding at most `capacity` of them. Return the new history after using `id` - it goes to the front, any earlier occurrence of it disappears, and the result is trimmed to `capacity` by dropping from the end. Do not modify the array you were given. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: Removing the old occurrence before trimming is what stops one id occupying two slots, and trimming last is what makes an eviction happen only when a genuinely new id arrives. The array here is the semantics, not the implementation - the Trial demands the same rules at $O(1)$ per use, which is what forces the list-plus-map pairing.

trial.prompt:
**The Trial.** Build the job vault: a scheduler that answers three different questions about the same jobs, each of them cheaply. Write `runVault(capacity, commands)`. `capacity` is a positive integer, `commands` is an array of command arrays, and the return value is an array holding **one result per command, in order**. Nothing survives between calls to `runVault`; the acceptance tests are the whole specification.

A job has an `id` and an integer `priority`, where a **smaller** priority is more urgent. A job is **pending** from the moment it is submitted until it is run or cancelled.

- `["submit", id, priority]` - make the job pending and return `true`. If a job with that id is already pending, change nothing and return `false`. An id that has already been run or cancelled may be submitted again, at any priority.
- `["cancel", id]` - return `true` if that id was pending and is now cancelled, and `false` otherwise. The cancelled entry is **not** removed from the priority structure; it is discarded when it reaches the top.
- `["run"]` - run the pending job with the smallest priority, breaking ties towards the **earlier submission**, and return its id. Running it makes it no longer pending and records it in the history. Return `null` when nothing is pending.
- `["history"]` - return an array of the ids in the history, **most recently run first**. An id run again moves to the front rather than appearing twice, and when the history would exceed `capacity` the least recently run id is dropped.
- `["stats"]` - return `{ pending, heapSize, historySize }`: the number of pending jobs, the number of entries still held in the priority structure - **cancelled ones included, since they are only discarded on reaching the top** - and the number of ids in the history.

`heapSize` is what makes the lazy deletion observable, so it must report the real contents of your priority structure rather than a recomputed count of live jobs. Every rule above is exercised by the tests below, and nothing is hidden from you.

tests.label: priority order first, then an empty vault returns null
a duplicate submit is refused, and cancelling twice is not a second cancellation
stats sees the corpse: heapSize 2 against pending 1
capacity 2 evicts the least recently run, and an id may be submitted again
an id run twice moves to the front of the history instead of duplicating
run on an empty vault, with an empty history and empty stats
capacity 1 keeps only the most recent
equal priorities break on submission order, including jobs submitted later
a cancelled id resubmitted at a new priority: three entries held, two pending

trial.explain:
Three questions, three shapes, one set of jobs. The heap answers **what is most urgent** in $O(\log n)$, the hash index answers **is this id pending** in $O(1)$, and the linked list with its own map answers **what ran recently** in $O(1)$ per use - and none of the three can answer another's question without a linear scan. That is the entire argument for composing them instead of picking a favourite.

The joint carrying the most weight is the one between the heap and the index. Cancelling cannot reach into the heap, so it writes to the index and leaves a corpse behind, and `run` pops until it finds an entry the index still vouches for. `stats` exposes that on purpose: after cancelling one of two jobs, `heapSize` is 2 while `pending` is 1, so an implementation that deletes eagerly - or that recomputes `heapSize` from the live jobs - reports 1 and fails. The accounting is amortised rather than free: each entry is pushed once and discarded at most once, so $m$ commands still cost $O(m \log n)$ overall even when one `run` throws away many entries.

Two details decide whether the vault is deterministic at all. Ties on priority must break on submission order, which means the heap compares a `(priority, sequence)` pair rather than the priority alone - without the sequence, `submit d 5` then `submit c 5` may run either job and the same input gives different output on different days. And an id run twice must **move** within the history rather than be inserted again; a duplicate leaves the map pointing at a node the list has forgotten, and the next eviction drops the wrong entry. Resubmission after a run is the case that ties everything together: the id is gone from the index, absent from the heap, and present in the history, so all three structures have to agree about a job that has lived twice.
